Authentication and authorisation flow\r\n\r\n```mermaid\r\nsequenceDiagram\r\n    actor User\r\n    participant UI as React frontend\r\n    participant Auth as Supabase Auth\r\n    participant API as Express API\r\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\r\n\r\n    User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\r\n    UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\r\n    Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\r\n    UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\r\n    API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\r\n    alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\r\n        API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\r\n    else Verified provider identity\r\n        Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\r\n        API->>DB: Upsert app_user; load status, role, and scoped grants\r\n        alt Account or permission check fails\r\n            API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\r\n        else Route and resource scope allowed\r\n            API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\r\n            API-->>UI: Safe response\r\n        end\r\n    end\r\n```\r\n\r\nImportant controls are:\r\n\r\n- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\r\n- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\r\n- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\r\n- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\r\n- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\r\n  if supported by the selected provider;\r\n- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\r\n  narrow administrative operations that require them; and\r\n- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\r\n\r\n## 7. Event submission to calculated statistics\r\n\r\n### End-to-end flow\r\n\r\n```mermaid\r\nsequenceDiagram\r\n    actor Submitter\r\n    participant UI as Frontend or API client\r\n    participant API as Handwritten API\r\n    participant AuthZ as Auth and permission middleware\r\n    participant Validate as Validation service\r\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\r\n    participant Jobs as Worker or in-process derivation\r\n    participant Files as File and export storage\r\n\r\n    Submitter->>UI: Enter events or choose JSON file\r\n    UI->>API: Submit payload, schema version, and bearer token\r\n    API->>AuthZ: Verify identity, approval, and target scope\r\n    AuthZ-->>API: Allowed submitter and effective scope\r\n    API->>API: Enforce content type and size, then calculate checksum\r\n    API->>DB: Create RECEIVED submission with provenance\r\n    opt Raw source file retained\r\n        API->>Files: Store source object under generated identifier\r\n    end\r\n    API->>Validate: Structural, referential, sequence, and cricket-rule validation\r\n    alt Validation fails\r\n        Validate-->>DB: Store safe field and record-level errors\r\n        API-->>UI: 422 with actionable validation result\r\n    else Valid but review required\r\n        Validate-->>DB: Mark PENDING_REVIEW\r\n        API-->>UI: 202 with submission status\r\n    else Accepted by policy or reviewer\r\n        Validate->>DB: Transactionally insert immutable event revisions and audit decision\r\n        DB-->>Jobs: Recalculate affected statistic scopes\r\n        Jobs->>DB: Read accepted current events\r\n        Jobs->>Jobs: Apply versioned deterministic definitions\r\n        Jobs->>DB: Upsert derived results and provenance\r\n        Jobs-->>API: Calculation complete or durable job status\r\n        API-->>UI: Accepted submission and statistic links\r\n    end\r\n```\r\n\r\nFor the Basic tier, bounded submissions and required fixture statistics may be validated and\r\nderived synchronously. Before processing becomes asynchronous, event acceptance and job\r\ncreation must be made atomic with a transactional outbox or equivalent pattern so an accepted\r\nevent cannot exist without its recalculation job.\r\n\r\n### Validation layers\r\n\r\n1. **Transport:** HTTPS, supported media type, request/file size, filename handling, and\r\n   decompression limits.\r\n2. **Contract:** versioned JSON schema, required fields, types, ranges, and unknown-field\r\n   policy.\r\n3. **Reference:** stable competition, fixture, team, and player identifiers; no name-based\r\n   player joins.\r\n4. **Cricket semantics:** innings/delivery ordering, team membership, extras, wickets,\r\n   super-over flags, miscounted overs, outcome forms, and other approved vocabulary.\r\n5. **Idempotency:** source reference, revision, checksum, and natural event identity prevent\r\n   duplicate ingestion while allowing corrections.\r\n6. **Permission:** submitter grant covers every target resource in the submission.\r\n7. **Review:** policy determines whether a structurally valid submission can be auto-accepted\r\n   or needs an independent reviewer.\r\n\r\nValidation errors are stored against the submission and returned without exposing internal\r\nqueries or secrets. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\r\naccepted records or none of them.\r\n\r\n### Corrections and derivation\r\n\r\nDelivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\r\nlive revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\r\nreads only the approved current-event view.\r\n\r\nRequired statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. The engine must cover\r\nthe event-model rules already approved in #27, including wides and balls faced, bowler extras,\r\nnon-boundary flags, innings-level penalty runs, actual legal-ball counts, stable player IDs,\r\nbowler-credit dismissal kinds, and the agreed super-over convention.\r\n\r\nEach stored result identifies:\r\n\r\n- statistic definition and version;\r\n- scope, such as fixture, innings, player, season, or career;\r\n- input event revision set or reproducible data version;\r\n- calculation status and timestamp; and\r\n- value and units.\r\n\r\nA correction marks only dependent results stale, recalculates them, and invalidates matching\r\ncache keys. Consumers must never observe a cache entry for a superseded data/definition\r\nversion.\r\n\r\n## 8. Files, datasets, and external integration\r\n\r\n### Uploads and source artefacts\r\n\r\n- Uploads enter through the backend; the browser never receives storage write credentials.\r\n- The API allow-lists formats, sanitises display names, ignores client filesystem paths,\r\n  generates object identifiers, enforces compressed and expanded size limits, and calculates\r\n  SHA-256 checksums.\r\n- PostgreSQL stores the submission, checksum, media type, object reference, source/retrieval\r\n  metadata, validation status, and owner. Object storage holds large bytes when selected.\r\n- Duplicate checksums are not sufficient by themselves: source reference and source revision\r\n  determine whether a file is a replay, correction, or different fixture.\r\n- Retention, malware scanning, and deletion rules must be agreed before arbitrary public file\r\n  uploads are enabled.\r\n\r\n### Dataset exports\r\n\r\nSmall filtered exports may stream from the API. Large or full releases become worker jobs and\r\nreturn `202 Accepted` with a status URL. Completed immutable releases include a version,\r\nscope, creation time, schema/statistic-definition versions, row or event counts, licence and\r\nprovenance notes, and checksums. Downloads use short-lived authorised links where necessary;\r\npublic releases may use stable public links.\r\n\r\n### External integration\r\n\r\nCricsheet's JSON archive is the approved historical source and already has a reproducible\r\ndownload and manifest process. It is a file feed, not a substitute for the project's required\r\nruntime external API integration. The team must select a relevant API based on stakeholder\r\nvalue, licence, T20 coverage, quotas, correction behaviour, and testability.\r\n\r\nAll providers are isolated behind adapters that convert external payloads into the internal\r\nsubmission contract. Provider calls use secret management, explicit timeouts, bounded retries\r\nwith jitter, rate-limit handling, circuit breaking where appropriate, schema checks, and\r\nobservable failures. Raw provider references, retrieval time, licence, version, and checksum\r\nare retained for provenance. An unavailable provider must degrade only the dependent feature,\r\nnot health checks, historical statistics, or unrelated API routes.\r\n\r\n## 9. Deployment and CI/CD\r\n\r\n```mermaid\r\nflowchart LR\r\n    Dev[Short-lived branch] --> PR[Gitea Pull Request]\r\n    PR --> CI[CI: install, structure, format,<br/>lint, typecheck, test, build]\r\n    CI --> Review[Peer review and approval]\r\n    Review --> Main[Protected main branch]\r\n    Main --> FE[Frontend deployment<br/>Azure App Service]\r\n    Main --> BE[Backend deployment<br/>Azure App Service]\r\n    Main --> Docs[MkDocs build and<br/>Cloudflare Pages deployment]\r\n    Migration[Reviewed SQL migrations] --> DB[(Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL)]\r\n    BE --> DB\r\n    FE --> BE\r\n    Secrets[Environment-specific secret stores] -.-> FE\r\n    Secrets -.-> BE\r\n```\r\n\r\n### Environments and deployment units\r\n\r\n- **Local:** Vite frontend on port 5173 and Express API on port 3000 run as separate\r\n  processes. Developers use safe environment placeholders and either shared development\r\n  services or an approved isolated local stack.\r\n- **Development:** the frontend and backend currently target separate Azure App Services.\r\n  PostgreSQL is hosted by Supabase in Frankfurt and reached by the backend over the TLS\r\n  Supavisor session pooler. The documentation site is deployed separately to Cloudflare\r\n  Pages.\r\n- **Preview/test:** Pull Requests always receive CI verification. Automated per-PR application\r\n  previews are desirable but not yet established.\r\n- **Production:** service names, database plan/region, storage, secrets, observability,\r\n  backups, and rollback procedures require a production decision record before release.\r\n\r\nFrontend configuration contains only browser-safe API and auth settings. Backend settings\r\ncontain `DATABASE_URL`, auth verification settings, allowed origins, external API keys, and\r\nfuture queue/storage credentials. Gitea Action secrets or platform secret stores provide\r\ndeployment credentials. Real secrets are never committed.\r\n\r\n### Pipeline controls\r\n\r\nThe existing Pull Request workflow uses Node.js 20, runs `npm ci`, then `npm run check`. The\r\nrepository check verifies required files, formatting, lint, TypeScript, automated tests, and\r\nall workspace builds. Before deployment is considered reliable, the pipeline must also:\r\n\r\n1. build MkDocs with `mkdocs build --strict`;\r\n2. correct the frontend/backend deployment path and workspace references so they match\r\n   `apps/frontend` and `apps/backend`;\r\n3. make deployments depend on the same green quality checks used for Pull Requests;\r\n4. run reviewed database migrations as an explicit, observable, and recoverable step rather\r\n   than on application startup;\r\n5. deploy immutable build output to the correct application;\r\n6. smoke-test frontend, API health, CORS, authentication callback, and database connectivity;\r\n7. record release identity and support rollback to the previous application version; and\r\n8. keep destructive migration changes backward-compatible across the deployment window.\r\n\r\nPath filters should deploy only affected units, while changes to contracts, root lockfiles,\r\nor shared configuration must trigger every dependent unit. The React frontend and Express backend are separate applications and separate deployment\r\n   units. They communicate through the documented HTTP API.\r\n2. PostgreSQL event records are the source of truth. Published statistics are derived values,\r\n   not independently entered totals.\r\n4. Authentication proves identity; backend authorisation separately determines roles,\r\n   approval state, and competition, season, or fixture scope.\r\n5. Every submission, correction, statistic, and export must retain provenance.\r\n6. Basic functionality is delivered before asynchronous, cached, live, or user-defined\r\n   functionality is introduced.\r\n7. Planned components must not be presented as implemented. Layout and spacing\r\n\r\n### 11.1 Spacing scale\r\n\r\nUse a 4 px base unit:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 80\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 11.2 Recommended content widths\r\n\r\n| Context                           | Maximum width |\r\n| --------------------------------- | ------------: |\r\n| Analytics application             |       1600 px |\r\n| Documentation / long-form content |       1100 px |\r\n| Form-focused flow                 |        760 px |\r\n| Standard modal                    |    720â€“900 px |\r\n\r\n### 11.3 Grid\r\n\r\nDesktop analytical screens may use a 12-column grid.\r\n\r\nUseful patterns include:\r\n\r\n- 8 columns for primary match content and 4 for supporting events;\r\n- 9 columns for charts and 3 for compact supporting tables;\r\n- four equal KPI cards;\r\n- full-width tables when comparison is the primary task.\r\n\r\n### 11.4 Responsive behaviour\r\n\r\nUse content-driven breakpoints. Starting values:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nSmall:   below 640 px\r\nMedium:  640â€“899 px\r\nLarge:   900â€“1199 px\r\nWide:    1200 px and above\r\n```\r\n\r\nStack dashboard regions before shrinking typography below usable sizes.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 12. Cricket data visualisation\r\n\r\n### 14.1 Chart palette\r\n\r\n| Role                    | Day Match       | Night Match     |\r\n| ----------------------- | --------------- | --------------- |\r\n| Current/selected series | Crease Green    | Powerplay Lime  |\r\n| Comparison series       | Analysis Cyan   | Review Cyan     |\r\n| Historical/unselected   | Scorebook Grey  | Commentary Grey |\r\n| Wicket/anomaly          | Boundary Orange | Boundary Orange |\r\n| Invalid/error state     | Rejected Red    | Rejected Red    |\r\n\r\n### 14.2 Chart rules\r\n\r\n- Start with the analytical question, not the chart type.\r\n- Avoid rainbow palettes.\r\n- Use line style, marker shape or opacity in addition to colour.\r\n- State units and ranges explicitly.\r\n- Label decisive points directly where practical.\r\n- Keep tooltips keyboard accessible where practical.\r\n- Provide text equivalents for important conclusions.\r\n- Do not delay access to data while a decorative animation completes.\r\n\r\n### 14.3 Cricket-specific conventions\r\n\r\nApproved visual patterns include:\r\n\r\n- orange wickets or decisive events;\r\n- green/lime for the selected innings or player;\r\n- cyan for comparison data;\r\n- a crease line for a target or benchmark;\r\n- ordered delivery events entering in source order.\r\n\r\nDo not use an error colour simply because it matches a team kit.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 15. Typography\r\n\r\n### 10.1 Font families\r\n\r\n| Role                                  | Font             |\r\n| ------------------------------------- | ---------------- |\r\n| Display headings and major statistics | Barlow Condensed |\r\n| Interface and body text               | IBM Plex Sans    |\r\n| API paths, IDs and technical values   | IBM Plex Mono    |\r\n\r\nApproved weights:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBarlow Condensed: 500, 600, 700\r\nIBM Plex Sans: 400, 500, 600\r\nIBM Plex Mono: 400, 500\r\n```\r\n\r\nProduction font loading must be treated as a documented frontend dependency. Prefer package-managed or self-hosted fonts over an undeclared third-party runtime dependency.\r\n\r\n### 10.2 Type scale\r\n\r\n| Style           | Size / line-height | Weight | Typical use            |\r\n| --------------- | ------------------ | -----: | ---------------------- |\r\n| Display         | 64 / 64            |    700 | Live score             |\r\n| Page heading    | 48 / 52            |    700 | Page title             |\r\n| Section heading | 30 / 34            |    600 | Dashboard section      |\r\n| Card heading    | 22 / 26            |    600 | Panel title            |\r\n| KPI value       | 40 / 42            |    600 | Key statistic          |\r\n| Body            | 16 / 24            |    400 | Main content           |\r\n| Small body      | 14 / 20            |    400 | Supporting content     |\r\n| Label           | 12 / 16            |    600 | Metadata               |\r\n| Technical       | 13 / 20            |    400 | Endpoint, ID, checksum |\r\n\r\n### 10.3 Typography rules\r\n\r\n- Use tabular numerals for scores, rates and data tables.\r\n- Use condensed typography for display values, not paragraphs.\r\n- Use uppercase only for short labels and compact navigation.\r\n- Keep normal body text at 16 px where practical.\r\n- Do not make every number lime or green.\r\n- Use IBM Plex Mono only where monospacing communicates meaning.\r\n- The logo wordmark is artwork; do not recreate it using Barlow Condensed.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 11. Layout and spacing\r\n\r\n### 11.1 Spacing scale\r\n\r\nUse a 4 px base unit:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 80\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 11.2 Recommended content widths\r\n\r\n| Context                           | Maximum width |\r\n| --------------------------------- | ------------: |\r\n| Analytics application             |       1600 px |\r\n| Documentation / long-form content |       1100 px |\r\n| Form-focused flow                 |        760 px |\r\n| Standard modal                    |    720â€“900 px |\r\n\r\n### 11.3 Grid\r\n\r\nDesktop analytical screens may use a 12-column grid.\r\n\r\nUseful patterns include:\r\n\r\n- 8 columns for primary match content and 4 for supporting events;\r\n- 9 columns for charts and 3 for compact supporting tables;\r\n- four equal KPI cards;\r\n- full-width tables when comparison is the primary task.\r\n\r\n### 11.4 Responsive behaviour\r\n\r\nUse content-driven breakpoints. Starting values:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nSmall:   below 640 px\r\nMedium:  640â€“899 px\r\nLarge:   900â€“1199 px\r\nWide:    1200 px and above\r\n```\r\n\r\nStack dashboard regions before shrinking typography below usable sizes.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 12. Shape and surface language\r\n\r\n### 12.1 Corners\r\n\r\n| Element                   | Radius |\r\n| ------------------------- | -----: |\r\n| Inputs and small controls |   6 px |\r\n| Standard cards            |  10 px |\r\n| Large overlays            |  16 px |\r\n\r\nFully rounded pills are reserved for controls or statuses where the shape has a clear purpose.\r\n\r\n### 12.2 Signature clipped corner\r\n\r\nFeatured match cards, logo tiles and selected hero surfaces may use one clipped bottom-right corner.\r\n\r\nDo not apply clipped corners to every container.\r\n\r\n### 12.3 Borders and elevation\r\n\r\n- Use 1 px borders for structural separation.\r\n- Use shadows to communicate elevation, not decoration.\r\n- Day Match shadows are broad and low-opacity.\r\n- Night Match shadows are restrained and dark.\r\n- Avoid glowing card borders.\r\n- Avoid glassmorphism as the standard card language.\r\n\r\n### 12.4 Crease line\r\n\r\nA 2â€“3 px line is a recurring visual device.\r\n\r\nAppropriate uses:\r\n\r\n- active navigation;\r\n- selected KPI card;\r\n- chart target or benchmark;\r\n- score transition;\r\n- section accent.\r\n\r\nDo not use it between every row.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 13. Core interface components\r\n\r\n### 13.1 Buttons\r\n\r\n#### Primary\r\n\r\nDay Match:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBackground: Crease Green\r\nText: white\r\n```\r\n\r\nNight Match:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBackground: Powerplay Lime\r\nText: Night Match\r\n```\r\n\r\nUse one dominant primary action per local region.\r\n\r\n#### Secondary\r\n\r\nUse:\r\n\r\n- surface background;\r\n- visible border;\r\n- primary text;\r\n- primary-colour focus/hover treatment.\r\n\r\n#### Destructive\r\n\r\nUse error styling only for genuinely destructive actions.\r\n\r\nIrreversible actions require confirmation.\r\n\r\n### 13.2 Cards\r\n\r\nCards should:\r\n\r\n- use solid surfaces;\r\n- group related information;\r\n- have a clear hierarchy;\r\n- avoid unnecessary icons;\r\n- use spacing before heavy shadows.\r\n\r\nDo not create a card solely to place a border around one line of text.\r\n\r\n### 13.3 Navigation\r\n\r\n- Desktop may use a compact left rail or top navigation.\r\n- Mobile navigation must remain understandable without relying only on icon familiarity.\r\n- The active state uses a soft selected surface plus the crease-line accent.\r\n- Navigation remains stable during page transitions.\r\n\r\n### 13.4 Tables\r\n\r\n- Left-align entity names.\r\n- Right-align numeric values.\r\n- Use tabular numerals.\r\n- Use subtle row separators.\r\n- Keep long table headers sticky where helpful.\r\n- Support horizontal overflow deliberately on small screens.\r\n- Do not turn every value into a badge.\r\n\r\n### 13.5 Forms\r\n\r\n- Keep labels visible above inputs.\r\n- Placeholder text does not replace a label.\r\n- Validation identifies the exact issue and location.\r\n- Required/error state is not communicated by colour alone.\r\n- Submission flows must show progress and actionable validation results.\r\n\r\n### 13.6 Loading and system states\r\n\r\nEvery data-driven screen must have deliberate states for:\r\n\r\n- loading;\r\n- empty results;\r\n- validation failure;\r\n- general error;\r\n- unauthorised access;\r\n- unavailable/offline backend;\r\n- partial data where the API explicitly supports it.\r\n\r\nDo not use an indefinite full-page spinner where useful structure can be rendered immediately.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 14. Cricket data visualisation\r\n\r\n### 14.1 Chart palette\r\n\r\n| Role                    | Day Match       | Night Match     |\r\n| ----------------------- | --------------- | --------------- |\r\n| Current/selected series | Crease Green    | Powerplay Lime  |\r\n| Comparison series       | Analysis Cyan   | Review Cyan     |\r\n| Historical/unselected   | Scorebook Grey  | Commentary Grey |\r\n| Wicket/anomaly          | Boundary Orange | Boundary Orange |\r\n| Invalid/error state     | Rejected Red    | Rejected Red    |\r\n\r\n### 14.2 Chart rules\r\n\r\n- Start with the analytical question, not the chart type.\r\n- Avoid rainbow palettes.\r\n- Use line style, marker shape or opacity in addition to colour.\r\n- State units and ranges explicitly.\r\n- Label decisive points directly where practical.\r\n- Keep tooltips keyboard accessible where practical.\r\n- Provide text equivalents for important conclusions.\r\n- Do not delay access to data while a decorative animation completes.\r\n\r\n### 14.3 Cricket-specific conventions\r\n\r\nApproved visual patterns include:\r\n\r\n- orange wickets or decisive events;\r\n- green/lime for the selected innings or player;\r\n- cyan for comparison data;\r\n- a crease line for a target or benchmark;\r\n- ordered delivery events entering in source order.\r\n\r\nDo not use an error colour simply because it matches a team kit.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 15. Motion system\r\n\r\n### 15.1 Motion character\r\n\r\n**Sharp acceleration, controlled stop.**\r\n\r\nMotion should make the interface feel responsive rather than decorative.\r\n\r\n### 15.2 Timing\r\n\r\n| Interaction            |   Duration |\r\n| ---------------------- | ---------: |\r\n| Hover / press feedback |  90â€“140 ms |\r\n| Tooltip / dropdown     | 140â€“180 ms |\r\n| Card / row entry       | 180â€“240 ms |\r\n| Page transition        | 220â€“320 ms |\r\n| Chart reveal           | 300â€“500 ms |\r\n| Modal opening          | 220â€“280 ms |\r\n\r\n### 15.3 Easing\r\n\r\n```css\r\n--ease-fast: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1);\r\n--ease-hit: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 15.4 Signature animations\r\n\r\n#### Score update\r\n\r\n1. Old value moves up by no more than 4 px and fades.\r\n2. New value enters from below.\r\n3. The crease line flashes once.\r\n4. Total duration stays below 500 ms.\r\n\r\n#### Delivery insertion\r\n\r\nA new delivery enters with:\r\n\r\n- 6â€“8 px vertical movement;\r\n- short opacity transition;\r\n- no layout-blocking delay.\r\n\r\n#### Wicket\r\n\r\nUse one orange pulse or narrow strike.\r\n\r\nDo not shake the screen or use confetti.\r\n\r\n#### Page transition\r\n\r\nFade and move the primary content by no more than 8 px.\r\n\r\nDo not move persistent navigation.\r\n\r\n#### Chart reveal\r\n\r\nThe selected line may draw left-to-right once on first appearance.\r\n\r\nFiltering or refreshing data should update promptly rather than replay a long entrance sequence.\r\n\r\n### 15.5 Motion restrictions\r\n\r\nDo not:\r\n\r\n- bounce cards continuously;\r\n- use decorative parallax behind data;\r\n- stagger a dashboard for long periods;\r\n- animate every value on every render;\r\n- block interaction while an animation finishes;\r\n- change layout dimensions significantly on hover.\r\n\r\n### 15.6 Reduced motion\r\n\r\nRespect the userâ€™s reduced-motion preference:\r\n\r\n```css\r\n@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {\r\n  *,\r\n  *::before,\r\n  *::after {\r\n    animation-duration: 0.001ms !important;\r\n    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;\r\n    transition-duration: 0.001ms !important;\r\n    scroll-behavior: auto !important;\r\n  }\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 16. Accessibility\r\n\r\nAccessibility is a project requirement and must be designed in from the start.\r\n\r\nThe teamâ€™s UI target is **WCAG 2.2 AA** unless a stricter project requirement supersedes it.\r\n\r\n### 16.1 Required practices\r\n\r\n- Verify text/background colour contrast.\r\n- Provide a visible keyboard focus state.\r\n- Prefer semantic HTML before adding ARIA.\r\n- Keep interactive controls keyboard operable.\r\n- Do not communicate state by colour alone.\r\n- Provide text alternatives for meaningful images.\r\n- Respect reduced-motion preferences.\r\n- Maintain usable touch targets.\r\n- Support browser zoom without loss of function.\r\n- Preserve table and chart meaning on small screens.\r\n- Test light and dark themes independently.\r\n\r\n### 16.2 Colour notes\r\n\r\nThe muted light-theme text token has been darkened to `#627078` so it remains suitable for normal-size text against the Warm Canvas.\r\n\r\nBoundary Orange is a brand accent on light surfaces, not a normal small-text colour.\r\n\r\nStatus colours should normally be paired with readable neutral text rather than used as the only text colour.\r\n\r\n### 16.3 Focus treatment\r\n\r\nUse a clearly visible 2 px focus ring with a 2 px offset.\r\n\r\nPreferred rings:\r\n\r\n- Day Match: Crease Green or Analysis Cyan.\r\n- Night Match: Powerplay Lime or Review Cyan.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 17. Iconography and imagery\r\n\r\n### 17.1 Icons\r\n\r\nUse:\r\n\r\n- simple outline icons;\r\n- consistent stroke weight;\r\n- consistent view-box sizing;\r\n- labels or accessible names for critical actions.\r\n\r\nAvoid mixing unrelated filled, outline and illustration styles.\r\n\r\n### 17.2 Cricket imagery\r\n\r\nPrefer:\r\n\r\n- real data;\r\n- scorecards;\r\n- field diagrams;\r\n- delivery trajectories;\r\n- the approved player mark;\r\n- licensed authentic photography where useful.\r\n\r\nAvoid:\r\n\r\n- generic trophy graphics;\r\n- crossed bats;\r\n- decorative shields;\r\n- fake 3D cricket balls;\r\n- arbitrary stadium imagery;\r\n- AI-generated players presented as real athletes.\r\n\r\n### 17.3 Photography\r\n\r\nWhen photography is used:\r\n\r\n- preserve authentic colours;\r\n- give overlaid text a solid or sufficiently opaque surface;\r\n- avoid heavy colour grading that competes with data;\r\n- do not place the logo over a face or visually complex focal point.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 18. Interface writing\r\n\r\nThe product voice is direct, informed and calm.\r\n\r\nGood:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nExplore matches\r\nView delivery data\r\nCompare innings\r\nExport dataset\r\nSubmission awaiting review\r\n12 events failed validation\r\n```\r\n\r\nAvoid:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nDive into the action\r\nUnleash next-level insights\r\nOops! Something went wrong\r\nYour data journey starts here\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 18.1 Error copy\r\n\r\nError messages should state:\r\n\r\n1. what failed;\r\n2. where it failed;\r\n3. what the user can do;\r\n4. whether data was accepted or published.\r\n\r\nExample:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nDelivery 43 is missing a striker identifier.\r\nNo events from this submission were published.\r\nAdd the identifier and submit the corrected file.\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 18.2 Cricket terminology\r\n\r\nUse recognised cricket terminology accurately.\r\n\r\nIf a term is likely to be unfamiliar to a general user, explain it with supporting copy or a tooltip rather than replacing it with vague language.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 19. Purpose\r\n\r\nThis document defines the project methodology that will be followed throughout the development of the Sport Analytics Tool.\r\n\r\nThe methodology establishes:\r\n\r\n- how project work will be planned;\r\n- how tasks will be recorded and prioritised;\r\n- how progress will be tracked;\r\n- how the team will communicate internally;\r\n- how stakeholder feedback will be collected and integrated;\r\n- how each sprint will be reviewed and closed;\r\n- how completed work will be verified; and\r\n- how changes to the methodology will be controlled.\r\n\r\nThe purpose of the methodology is to provide a consistent, visible and lightweight process for managing the project. It is intended to support effective collaboration without introducing unnecessary administrative work.\r\n\r\nAll team members are required to follow this methodology consistently.\r\n\r\n## 2. Selected Methodology\r\n\r\nThe team will use a **lightweight Scrumban methodology**.\r\n\r\nScrumban combines selected elements of Scrum and Kanban:\r\n\r\n- fixed project sprints are used for planning and review;\r\n- a visual Gitea Project board is used to track work continuously;\r\n- stakeholder feedback is incorporated throughout development;\r\n- work is completed in small, manageable tasks;\r\n- unnecessary Scrum roles, story points and daily meetings are avoided.\r\n\r\nThis methodology was selected because the project has formal sprint deadlines, while its detailed requirements and priorities may change following stakeholder feedback, technical investigation and testing.\r\n\r\nFull Scrum was not selected because daily standups, formal roles and detailed estimation would create unnecessary overhead for the size and duration of this project.\r\n\r\nPure Kanban was not selected because the project is structured around assessed sprint milestones and therefore requires clear sprint planning, review and reflection.\r\n\r\nThe selected methodology provides enough structure to demonstrate planning, stakeholder interaction, progress tracking and continuous improvement while remaining simple enough to follow consistently.\r\n\r\n## 3. Project Management Platform\r\n\r\nGitea will act as the teamâ€™s primary source of truth for project work.\r\n\r\nThe team will use:\r\n\r\n- **Gitea Issues** for features, bugs, documentation, testing, research and technical tasks;\r\n- **Gitea Projects** for the visual work board;\r\n- **Gitea Milestones** for Sprint 1, Sprint 2, Sprint 3 and the Final Submission;\r\n- **Gitea Pull Requests** for implementation review;\r\n- **repository documentation** for meeting notes, decisions and methodology records.\r\n\r\nImportant project decisions made in meetings, messages or informal discussions must be transferred to Gitea or the project documentation where they affect requirements, priorities, responsibilities or implementation.\r\n\r\n## 4. Project Board\r\n\r\nThe Gitea Project board will use the following columns:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBacklog\r\nReady\r\nIn Progress\r\nIn Review\r\nBlocked\r\nDone\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 4.1 Backlog\r\n\r\nThe `Backlog` contains identified work that has not yet been selected for active development.\r\n\r\nAn item may remain in the backlog where:\r\n\r\n- it is not yet a current priority;\r\n- further stakeholder clarification is required;\r\n- the task is optional;\r\n- the task belongs to a future sprint; or\r\n- the task requires further investigation before it can be prepared.\r\n\r\n### 4.2 Ready\r\n\r\nThe `Ready` column contains work that is sufficiently defined and can be started.\r\n\r\nAn issue may only move to `Ready` when it meets the teamâ€™s Definition of Ready.\r\n\r\n### 4.3 In Progress\r\n\r\nThe `In Progress` column contains work currently being completed.\r\n\r\nEach team member should normally have no more than one main issue in progress at a time. This work-in-progress limit is intended to encourage completion before additional work is started.\r\n\r\nA second small task may only be started where the primary issue is blocked or awaiting review.\r\n\r\n### 4.4 In Review\r\n\r\nThe `In Review` column contains work that has been completed by its assignee and is awaiting review, testing or approval.\r\n\r\nCode-related issues will normally enter this column once a Pull Request has been opened.\r\n\r\n### 4.5 Blocked\r\n\r\nThe `Blocked` column contains work that cannot continue.\r\n\r\nA blocked issue must include a comment explaining:\r\n\r\n- what is preventing progress;\r\n- what is required to remove the blocker;\r\n- who is responsible for the next action; and\r\n- when the issue will be reviewed again.\r\n\r\n### 4.6 Done\r\n\r\nThe `Done` column contains work that satisfies the teamâ€™s Definition of Done.\r\n\r\nAn issue may not be moved to `Done` merely because implementation has started or a partial result exists.\r\n\r\n## 5. Sprint Structure\r\n\r\nThe project will be organised around the following formal milestones:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nSprint 1\r\nSprint 2\r\nSprint 3\r\nFinal Submission\r\n```\r\n\r\nEach milestone period will be treated as a sprint.\r\n\r\nEvery sprint will include:\r\n\r\n1. sprint planning;\r\n2. continuous work tracking;\r\n3. weekly stakeholder interaction;\r\n4. a weekly team standup;\r\n5. development and review; and\r\n6. a brief sprint close-out.\r\n\r\nEach sprint will have a clear sprint goal that states the main outcome the team intends to achieve.\r\n\r\n## 6. Sprint Planning\r\n\r\nThe team will hold one sprint-planning meeting at the beginning of each sprint.\r\n\r\nThe meeting should normally last between 30 and 45 minutes.\r\n\r\nDuring sprint planning, the team will:\r\n\r\n1. agree on the sprint goal;\r\n2. review the project requirements;\r\n3. review stakeholder feedback;\r\n4. review incomplete work from the previous sprint;\r\n5. select issues from the backlog;\r\n6. confirm that selected issues meet the Definition of Ready;\r\n7. identify dependencies and technical risks;\r\n8. assign initial issue owners;\r\n9. allocate selected issues to the relevant Gitea milestone; and\r\n10. confirm the expected outcome of the sprint.\r\n\r\nA short sprint-planning record will be saved in the repository.\r\n\r\nThe record must include:\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n# Sprint Planning\r\n\r\n**Sprint:**  \r\n**Date:**  \r\n**Attendees:**\r\n\r\n## Sprint Goal\r\n\r\n## Selected Work\r\n\r\n## Key Risks and Dependencies\r\n\r\n## Decisions\r\n\r\n## Unresolved Questions\r\n```\r\n\r\nA full transcript of the meeting is not required.\r\n\r\n## 7. Weekly Stakeholder Meeting\r\n\r\nThe team will meet with the assigned stakeholder or tutor every Tuesday, where reasonably possible.\r\n\r\nThe meeting should normally last between 20 and 30 minutes.\r\n\r\nThe purpose of the stakeholder meeting is to:\r\n\r\n- demonstrate recent progress;\r\n- clarify requirements;\r\n- confirm priorities;\r\n- ask questions;\r\n- receive feedback;\r\n- discuss proposed changes;\r\n- identify missing requirements; and\r\n- confirm whether completed work meets expectations.\r\n\r\nThe team will prepare relevant demonstrations or questions before the meeting.\r\n\r\nA short stakeholder record must be saved after each meeting.\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n# Stakeholder Meeting\r\n\r\n**Date:**  \r\n**Attendees:**  \r\n**Purpose:**\r\n\r\n## Progress Demonstrated\r\n\r\n## Requirements Discussed\r\n\r\n## Feedback Received\r\n\r\n## Decisions\r\n\r\n## Actions\r\n\r\n## Related Gitea Issues\r\n\r\n- #...\r\n```\r\n\r\nStakeholder feedback that affects the project must result in one of the following:\r\n\r\n- an existing Gitea issue being updated;\r\n- a new Gitea issue being created;\r\n- an issue being reprioritised;\r\n- an acceptance criterion being clarified; or\r\n- a documented decision that no change will be made.\r\n\r\nRequirements may not be changed silently.\r\n\r\nWhere a Tuesday meeting cannot take place, the team may use a structured written update or arrange the meeting on another day during the same week.\r\n\r\n## 8. Weekly Team Standup\r\n\r\nThe team will hold one internal standup every Thursday.\r\n\r\nThe standup should normally last no longer than 15 minutes.\r\n\r\nEach team member will answer:\r\n\r\n1. What have I completed since the previous standup?\r\n2. What am I currently working on?\r\n3. What will I complete next?\r\n4. Is anything blocking my progress?\r\n\r\nThe team will also briefly:\r\n\r\n- review the Gitea Project board;\r\n- check progress towards the sprint goal;\r\n- review actions arising from Tuesdayâ€™s stakeholder meeting;\r\n- identify delayed or blocked work;\r\n- confirm whether responsibilities need to change; and\r\n- identify any urgent issue requiring a separate discussion.\r\n\r\nThe standup is intended for coordination rather than detailed technical problem-solving. Longer discussions must take place after the standup with only the relevant team members.\r\n\r\nFormal minutes are not required for every standup. Gitea Issues\r\n\r\nEvery meaningful unit of project work must be recorded as a Gitea issue.\r\n\r\nExamples include:\r\n\r\n- new features;\r\n- bug fixes;\r\n- database changes;\r\n- API work;\r\n- user-interface work;\r\n- automated testing;\r\n- documentation;\r\n- CI/CD configuration;\r\n- technical research;\r\n- stakeholder-requested changes; and\r\n- project risks requiring action.\r\n\r\nEach issue must contain:\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n## Description\r\n\r\nExplain what must be completed.\r\n\r\n## Motivation\r\n\r\nExplain why the work is required.\r\n\r\n## Acceptance Criteria\r\n\r\n- [ ] Specific observable result\r\n- [ ] Relevant tests pass\r\n- [ ] Documentation is updated where applicable\r\n\r\n## Dependencies\r\n\r\nList related or blocking issues.\r\n\r\n## Evidence\r\n\r\nLink relevant designs, meeting notes, Pull Requests or test results.\r\n```\r\n\r\nEach issue must also have:\r\n\r\n- a clear title;\r\n- an assignee;\r\n- a sprint milestone;\r\n- an appropriate work-type label; and\r\n- an area label where relevant.\r\n\r\nSuggested work-type labels are:\r\n\r\n```text\r\ntype: feature\r\ntype: bug\r\ntype: documentation\r\ntype: testing\r\ntype: research\r\ntype: infrastructure\r\n```\r\n\r\nSuggested area labels are:\r\n\r\n```text\r\narea: frontend\r\narea: api\r\narea: database\r\narea: data\r\narea: infrastructure\r\narea: documentation\r\n```\r\n\r\nSuggested additional labels are:\r\n\r\n```text\r\npriority: high\r\nstatus: blocked\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe team will avoid creating unnecessary labels that are not used consistently.\r\n\r\n## 11. Task Size and Estimation\r\n\r\nThe team will not use story points or formal velocity calculations.\r\n\r\nIssues should normally be small enough to complete within one to three working days.\r\n\r\nAn issue should be divided into smaller issues where:\r\n\r\n- it contains several independent outcomes;\r\n- it is expected to take most of a sprint;\r\n- it cannot be reviewed effectively as one unit;\r\n- different team members can complete separate parts independently; or\r\n- its acceptance criteria are too broad.\r\n\r\nThe team may use simple labels such as `small`, `medium` and `large` where this is useful, but these labels are optional.\r\n\r\nThe purpose of task sizing is to keep work manageable rather than to produce detailed time estimates.\r\n\r\n## 12. Purpose\r\n\r\nThis document defines the Git methodology that will be followed throughout the development of the Sport Analytics Tool.\r\n\r\nThe methodology establishes:\r\n\r\n- when commits must be created;\r\n- how commit messages must be written;\r\n- when branches must be created;\r\n- how branches must be named;\r\n- when branches may be merged;\r\n- the requirements that must be met before merging;\r\n- when project versions must be created; and\r\n- how project versions must be named.\r\n\r\nThe purpose of the methodology is to maintain an organised repository, support effective collaboration, reduce merge conflicts, enable code review and provide traceability between requirements and their implementation.\r\n\r\nAll team members are required to apply this methodology consistently across all project repositories.\r\n\r\n## 2. Selected Methodology\r\n\r\nThe team will use **GitHub Flow adapted for Gitea**.\r\n\r\nUnder this methodology:\r\n\r\n1. `main` contains the latest reviewed and working version of the project.\r\n2. Each significant unit of work begins as a Gitea issue.\r\n3. A short-lived branch is created for the issue.\r\n4. Development is completed through small, meaningful commits.\r\n5. The branch, commits and Pull Request reference the issue.\r\n6. A Pull Request is reviewed before it is merged.\r\n7. Approved work is merged into `main`.\r\n8. Important milestone states are identified using Git tags.\r\n\r\nThis methodology was selected because it provides sufficient control, traceability and peer review without introducing unnecessary permanent branches or administrative processes.\r\n\r\nA more complex methodology, such as Git Flow, would require additional `develop`, `release` and `hotfix` branches. These branches are not necessary for the size, duration or release structure of this project.\r\n\r\nThe selected methodology is therefore intended to remain lightweight enough to be followed consistently by all team members.\r\n\r\n## 3. The `main` Branch\r\n\r\nThe `main` branch represents the latest integrated, reviewed and working version of the project.\r\n\r\nThe following rules apply to `main`:\r\n\r\n- Direct development on `main` is prohibited.\r\n- Direct pushes to `main` are prohibited.\r\n- Changes may only enter `main` through an approved Gitea Pull Request.\r\n- `main` must remain in a buildable and working state.\r\n- Force pushes to `main` are prohibited.\r\n- Required automated checks must pass before a Pull Request may be merged.\r\n- Milestone version tags may only be created from `main`.\r\n\r\nThe `main` branch will be protected using Giteaâ€™s branch-protection settings where these settings are available.\r\n\r\n## 4. Gitea Issues and Traceability\r\n\r\nEvery significant development task must begin as a Gitea issue.\r\n\r\nAn issue must contain:\r\n\r\n- a clear title;\r\n- a description of the required work;\r\n- acceptance criteria;\r\n- an assigned team member;\r\n- the relevant sprint milestone; and\r\n- appropriate labels.\r\n\r\nExamples of work that requires an issue include:\r\n\r\n- implementing a feature;\r\n- fixing a bug;\r\n- creating or changing an API endpoint;\r\n- changing the database schema;\r\n- adding automated tests;\r\n- configuring infrastructure or CI/CD;\r\n- completing substantial documentation; and\r\n- performing a technical investigation that will influence development.\r\n\r\nVery small corrections, such as correcting a spelling error, may be included in an existing relevant issue.\r\n\r\nEach significant change will follow the traceability chain below:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nGitea issue â†’ branch â†’ commits â†’ Pull Request â†’ merge\r\n```\r\n\r\nFor example, work related to issue `#12` would be recorded as follows:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nIssue:        #12 Validate event submissions\r\nBranch:       feat/12-validate-event-submissions\r\nCommit body:  Refs #12\r\nPull Request: #12 Validate event submissions\r\nPR body:      Closes #12\r\n```\r\n\r\nThis process allows the team to trace completed work back to its original requirement, implementation, review and final integration.\r\n\r\n## 5. A season is presented\r\nin its competition context rather than as an isolated technical resource.\r\n\r\n### User-facing naming and internal references\r\n\r\nReadable names are the primary identity in headings, links, filters, cards, breadcrumbs, accessible\r\nnames, and related-record sections.\r\n\r\n| Concept     | Primary user-facing identity       | Human-readable disambiguation                        | Internal-only reference examples                 |\r\n| ----------- | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |\r\n| Competition | Competition name                   | Gender or format only when needed                    | `competitionId`; route and query values          |\r\n| Season      | Season label with competition name | Year/date range or format when available             | `seasonId`; `competitionId`                      |\r\n| Fixture     | Team name versus team name         | Date; competition; season; match type                | `fixtureId`; statistic and event identifiers     |\r\n| Team        | Team name                          | Competition; season; gender or team type when needed | `competitorId`; API resource name `competitor`   |\r\n| Player      | Player display name                | Team; fixture; season or role when available         | `participantId`; API resource name `participant` |\r\n\r\nStable identifiers, cursors, API resource terminology, and query values remain available for React\r\nkeys, URL construction, routing, API requests, caching, and telemetry. A named fixture in its embedded history opens\r\nthe fixture overview in the second interaction; fixture statistics are then already present.\r\n\r\n### Three-purposeful-interaction requirement\r\n\r\nMeasurement begins after the appropriate public entry page has loaded:\r\n\r\n- competition information starts at the Competitions entry page;\r\n- team information starts at Teams;\r\n- player information starts at Players; and\r\n- a known fixture may start at Fixtures.\r\n\r\nA purposeful interaction is one user activation that changes the visible result set, reveals\r\nrequired content, or navigates to another record. The earlier\r\nshared register remains available while its entries are migrated.\r\n# Git Methodology\r\n\r\n| Document Information | Details                       |\r\n| -------------------- | ----------------------------- |\r\n| Project              | Sport Analytics Tool          |\r\n| Platform             | Gitea                         |\r\n| Methodology          | GitHub Flow adapted for Gitea |\r\n| Document Version     | 1.0                           |\r\n| Date                 | 4 August 2026                 |\r\n| Status               | Approved for Use              |\r\n| Team                 | Git Push Pray                 |\r\n\r\n## 1. Purpose\r\n\r\nThis document defines the Git methodology that will be followed throughout the development of the Sport Analytics Tool.\r\n\r\nThe methodology establishes:\r\n\r\n- when commits must be created;\r\n- how commit messages must be written;\r\n- when branches must be created;\r\n- how branches must be named;\r\n- when branches may be merged;\r\n- the requirements that must be met before merging;\r\n- when project versions must be created; and\r\n- how project versions must be named.\r\n\r\nThe purpose of the methodology is to maintain an organised repository, support effective collaboration, reduce merge conflicts, enable code review and provide traceability between requirements and their implementation.\r\n\r\nAll team members are required to apply this methodology consistently across all project repositories.\r\n\r\n## 2. Selected Methodology\r\n\r\nThe team will use **GitHub Flow adapted for Gitea**.\r\n\r\nUnder this methodology:\r\n\r\n1. `main` contains the latest reviewed and working version of the project.\r\n2. Each significant unit of work begins as a Gitea issue.\r\n3. A short-lived branch is created for the issue.\r\n4. Development is completed through small, meaningful commits.\r\n5. The branch, commits and Pull Request reference the issue.\r\n6. A Pull Request is reviewed before it is merged.\r\n7. Approved work is merged into `main`.\r\n8. Important milestone states are identified using Git tags.\r\n\r\nThis methodology was selected because it provides sufficient control, traceability and peer review without introducing unnecessary permanent branches or administrative processes.\r\n\r\nA more complex methodology, such as Git Flow, would require additional `develop`, `release` and `hotfix` branches. These branches are not necessary for the size, duration or release structure of this project.\r\n\r\nThe selected methodology is therefore intended to remain lightweight enough to be followed consistently by all team members.\r\n\r\n## 3. The `main` Branch\r\n\r\nThe `main` branch represents the latest integrated, reviewed and working version of the project.\r\n\r\nThe following rules apply to `main`:\r\n\r\n- Direct development on `main` is prohibited.\r\n- Direct pushes to `main` are prohibited.\r\n- Changes may only enter `main` through an approved Gitea Pull Request.\r\n- `main` must remain in a buildable and working state.\r\n- Force pushes to `main` are prohibited.\r\n- Required automated checks must pass before a Pull Request may be merged.\r\n- Milestone version tags may only be created from `main`.\r\n\r\nThe `main` branch will be protected using Giteaâ€™s branch-protection settings where these settings are available.\r\n\r\n## 4. Gitea Issues and Traceability\r\n\r\nEvery significant development task must begin as a Gitea issue.\r\n\r\nAn issue must contain:\r\n\r\n- a clear title;\r\n- a description of the required work;\r\n- acceptance criteria;\r\n- an assigned team member;\r\n- the relevant sprint milestone; and\r\n- appropriate labels.\r\n\r\nExamples of work that requires an issue include:\r\n\r\n- implementing a feature;\r\n- fixing a bug;\r\n- creating or changing an API endpoint;\r\n- changing the database schema;\r\n- adding automated tests;\r\n- configuring infrastructure or CI/CD;\r\n- completing substantial documentation; and\r\n- performing a technical investigation that will influence development.\r\n\r\nVery small corrections, such as correcting a spelling error, may be included in an existing relevant issue.\r\n\r\nEach significant change will follow the traceability chain below:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nGitea issue â†’ branch â†’ commits â†’ Pull Request â†’ merge\r\n```\r\n\r\nFor example, work related to issue `#12` would be recorded as follows:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nIssue:        #12 Validate event submissions\r\nBranch:       feat/12-validate-event-submissions\r\nCommit body:  Refs #12\r\nPull Request: #12 Validate event submissions\r\nPR body:      Closes #12\r\n```\r\n\r\nThis process allows the team to trace completed work back to its original requirement, implementation, review and final integration.\r\n\r\n## 5. When to Create a Branch\r\n\r\nA branch must be created when a team member begins work on a Gitea issue involving code, tests, configuration or substantial documentation.\r\n\r\nBefore creating a branch:\r\n\r\n1. The related Gitea issue must exist.\r\n2. The issue must have a clear description.\r\n3. The issue must contain acceptance criteria.\r\n4. The issue must have an assignee.\r\n5. The issue must be assigned to the relevant sprint milestone.\r\n6. The developer must update their local copy of `main`.\r\n\r\nThe branch must be created from the latest version of `main`.\r\n\r\n```bash\r\ngit switch main\r\ngit pull origin main\r\ngit switch -c feat/12-validate-event-submissions\r\n```\r\n\r\nA branch should normally address one Gitea issue.\r\n\r\nWhere two issues cannot reasonably be separated, both issue numbers must be identified in the Pull Request description.\r\n\r\nBranches must be short-lived. A normal branch should be completed within five working days. A branch may not remain open beyond the sprint in which it was created unless the delay and reason are recorded in the related issue.\r\n\r\nIf a branch becomes too large to review effectively, the work must be divided into smaller issues and branches.\r\n\r\n## 6. How to Name Branches\r\n\r\nBranch names must follow this format:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n<type>/<issue-number>-<short-description>\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe approved branch types are:\r\n\r\n| Type       | Purpose                                          |\r\n| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ |\r\n| `feat`     | New functionality                                |\r\n| `fix`      | Correction of incorrect behaviour                |\r\n| `docs`     | Documentation changes                            |\r\n| `test`     | Test creation or modification                    |\r\n| `refactor` | Code restructuring without a change in behaviour |\r\n| `chore`    | Maintenance, setup or configuration              |\r\n| `ci`       | Continuous integration or deployment changes     |\r\n\r\nExamples include:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nfeat/12-validate-event-submissions\r\nfix/18-prevent-duplicate-statistics\r\ndocs/21-add-api-documentation\r\ntest/24-test-event-validation\r\nrefactor/31-extract-statistics-service\r\nchore/7-configure-project\r\nci/9-add-backend-pipeline\r\n```\r\n\r\nBranch names must:\r\n\r\n- use lowercase letters;\r\n- contain the related issue number;\r\n- separate words using hyphens;\r\n- contain no spaces;\r\n- use a concise but meaningful description; and\r\n- reflect the main purpose of the branch.\r\n\r\n## 7. When to Commit\r\n\r\nA commit must be created whenever one small, logically complete unit of work has been completed.\r\n\r\nEach commit must:\r\n\r\n- represent one identifiable change;\r\n- relate to the issue assigned to the branch;\r\n- leave the affected section of the project in a working state;\r\n- not knowingly introduce compilation or build failures;\r\n- not knowingly cause existing tests to fail;\r\n- exclude unrelated changes; and\r\n- be understandable independently of later commits.\r\n\r\nExamples of suitable commits include:\r\n\r\n- creating the fixture database model;\r\n- adding event-schema validation;\r\n- implementing one API endpoint;\r\n- correcting one calculation error;\r\n- adding tests for one endpoint;\r\n- updating the setup instructions for one service.\r\n\r\nA commit must not combine unrelated work. For example, a single commit should not contain an unrelated API feature, user-interface redesign and documentation rewrite.\r\n\r\nDevelopers must commit regularly and must not wait until an entire sprint or large feature has been completed before creating a commit.\r\n\r\nTemporary commits may be used while work is in progress. However, commits with unclear messages such as `WIP`, `fix stuff` or `more changes` must not remain in a branch submitted for final review.\r\n\r\n## 8. How to Write Commit Messages\r\n\r\nThe team will use a simplified Conventional Commit format.\r\n\r\nThe required format is:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n<type>(<scope>): <description>\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe scope may be omitted when it does not provide useful additional information:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n<type>: <description>\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 8.1 Approved Commit Types\r\n\r\n| Type       | Purpose                                           |\r\n| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------- |\r\n| `feat`     | Adds new functionality                            |\r\n| `fix`      | Corrects incorrect behaviour                      |\r\n| `docs`     | Changes documentation only                        |\r\n| `test`     | Adds or modifies tests                            |\r\n| `refactor` | Restructures code without changing behaviour      |\r\n| `chore`    | Changes maintenance, setup or configuration files |\r\n| `ci`       | Changes the CI/CD process                         |\r\n\r\n### 8.2 Commit Message Requirements\r\n\r\nThe commit description must:\r\n\r\n- begin with a lowercase verb;\r\n- state what the commit accomplishes;\r\n- be concise but specific;\r\n- use the imperative form; and\r\n- avoid vague descriptions.\r\n\r\nAcceptable commit messages include:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nfeat(api): add event submission endpoint\r\nfix(stats): prevent duplicate events from affecting totals\r\ntest(api): add invalid event submission cases\r\ndocs(setup): document local database configuration\r\nci: run backend tests on pull requests\r\n```\r\n\r\nUnacceptable commit messages include:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nupdated files\r\nfixed things\r\nmore work\r\nchanges\r\nfinal version\r\nstuff\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 8.3 Linking Commits to Issues\r\n\r\nEvery normal development commit must reference the related Gitea issue in its commit body.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nfeat(api): validate submitted event structure\r\n\r\nRefs #12\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe issue will normally be closed by the Pull Request rather than by an individual commit. This ensures that the issue remains open until all associated work has been reviewed and merged.\r\n\r\nMerge commits, automated dependency commits and automatically generated revert commits are exempt from the normal issue-reference requirement where a manual reference would not be appropriate.\r\n\r\n### 8.4 AI-Assisted Code\r\n\r\nWhere AI-generated code is included in a commit, the commit body must include the required tool and model attribution.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nfeat(api): validate submitted event structure\r\n\r\nRefs #12\r\nAssisted-by: ChatGPT-Web[GPT-5.6 Thinking]\r\n```\r\n\r\nOnly tools and models genuinely used in producing the code contained in that commit may be listed.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 9. When to Open a Pull Request\r\n\r\nA Pull Request must be opened when the work on a branch is ready for review.\r\n\r\nBefore opening a Pull Request, the author must:\r\n\r\n1. review the changes personally;\r\n2. update the branch with the latest version of `main`;\r\n3. resolve all merge conflicts;\r\n4. run the relevant tests locally;\r\n5. remove debugging code and unnecessary temporary files;\r\n6. confirm that the issueâ€™s acceptance criteria have been addressed;\r\n7. update relevant documentation;\r\n8. confirm that no credentials or sensitive information have been committed; and\r\n9. include the required AI attribution where applicable.\r\n\r\nA draft Pull Request may be opened earlier when feedback is required before the work is complete. A draft Pull Request must be clearly identified and may not be merged.\r\n\r\nThe Pull Request title must contain the related issue number:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n#12 Validate event submissions\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe Pull Request description must include:\r\n\r\n```markdown\r\n## Purpose\r\n\r\nExplain why the change is required.\r\n\r\n## Changes\r\n\r\nSummarise the main changes made.\r\n\r\n## Testing\r\n\r\nExplain how the change was tested.\r\n\r\n## Known Limitations\r\n\r\nList any remaining limitations, or state that none are known.\r\n\r\n## Related Issue\r\n\r\nCloses #12\r\n```\r\n\r\n## 10. When to Merge\r\n\r\nA branch may only be merged after its Pull Request has completed the required review and verification process.\r\n\r\nA developer may not merge their own Pull Request without approval from at least one other team member.\r\n\r\nThe team will use **merge commits** when merging Pull Requests into `main`.\r\n\r\nMerge commits were selected because they preserve:\r\n\r\n- the individual development commits;\r\n- the identity of the feature branch;\r\n- the Pull Request as a distinct unit of work; and\r\n- the relationship between the issue and its implementation.\r\n\r\nAfter a Pull Request has been merged:\r\n\r\n1. The related Gitea issue must be closed.\r\n2. The completed branch must be deleted from Gitea.\r\n3. The associated Project board item must be moved to `Done`.\r\n4. Any incomplete or follow-up work must be recorded as a new issue.\r\n\r\n## 11. Requirements for Merging\r\n\r\nA Pull Request may be merged only when all the following requirements have been satisfied.\r\n\r\n### 11.1 Issue and Scope\r\n\r\n- The Pull Request is linked to at least one Gitea issue.\r\n- The issueâ€™s acceptance criteria have been met.\r\n- The Pull Request contains no unrelated changes.\r\n- Any approved change in scope has been recorded in the issue.\r\n\r\n### 11.2 Description\r\n\r\n- The purpose of the change is explained.\r\n- The main implementation changes are summarised.\r\n- The testing process is described.\r\n- Known limitations are documented.\r\n- The related issue is identified using `Closes #<issue-number>`.\r\n\r\n### 11.3 Review\r\n\r\n- The author has reviewed their own changes.\r\n- At least one team member other than the author has reviewed the Pull Request.\r\n- At least one approval has been recorded.\r\n- All reviewer comments have been answered.\r\n- All requested changes have been implemented or formally resolved.\r\n- The reviewer has confirmed that the implementation matches its stated purpose.\r\n\r\n### 11.4 Testing and Quality\r\n\r\n- All relevant automated tests pass.\r\n- Existing tests continue to pass.\r\n- All required CI checks pass.\r\n- Formatting, linting and type-checking checks pass where configured.\r\n- The affected application or service builds successfully.\r\n- Deployment checks pass where the change affects deployment.\r\n- No unresolved merge conflicts remain.\r\n- No credentials, secrets or sensitive information are included.\r\n- No unnecessary generated or temporary files are included.\r\n\r\n### 11.5 Documentation\r\n\r\n- Relevant technical documentation has been updated.\r\n- Setup instructions have been updated where necessary.\r\n- API documentation has been updated where an endpoint or schema changed.\r\n- Database documentation has been updated where the schema changed.\r\n- AI assistance has been declared where required.\r\n\r\nA Pull Request that does not meet every applicable requirement must not be merged.\r\n\r\n## 12. When to Create a Version\r\n\r\nA project version will be created when the team reaches a formal assessed milestone and the corresponding code has been reviewed and stabilised.\r\n\r\nVersions will be created for:\r\n\r\n- Sprint 1;\r\n- Sprint 2;\r\n- Sprint 3; and\r\n- the final submission.\r\n\r\nA version may only be created when:\r\n\r\n1. All work included in the milestone has been merged into `main`.\r\n2. The milestone version builds successfully.\r\n3. All required automated checks pass.\r\n4. The team has reviewed the milestone state.\r\n5. Known defects and limitations have been documented.\r\n6. The exact commit being submitted has been confirmed.\r\n7. The repository documentation accurately reflects the submitted state.\r\n\r\nThe version will be recorded using an annotated Git tag created from `main`.\r\n\r\n## 13. How to Name Versions\r\n\r\nThe project will use descriptive milestone versioning.\r\n\r\nThe primary version tags will be:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nsprint-1\r\nsprint-2\r\nsprint-3\r\nfinal-submission\r\n```\r\n\r\nIf an authorised correction is required after a milestone version has been created, the corrected version will use a numbered revision:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nsprint-1.1\r\nsprint-1.2\r\n```\r\n\r\nAn existing tag may not be moved, renamed or overwritten. A new tag must be created so that the original submitted version remains available.\r\n\r\nDescriptive milestone versioning was selected because the projectâ€™s most significant development versions correspond directly with its assessed milestones. This makes versions clear to both the development team and project assessors.\r\n\r\n## 14. Standard Development Workflow\r\n\r\nAll significant work must follow the process below:\r\n\r\n1. Create a Gitea issue.\r\n2. Add a description and acceptance criteria.\r\n3. Assign the issue to a team member and sprint milestone.\r\n4. Update the local `main` branch.\r\n5. Create a branch containing the issue number.\r\n6. Complete the work using small, atomic commits.\r\n7. Reference the issue in each applicable commit.\r\n8. Test and review the work locally.\r\n9. Open a Pull Request linked to the issue.\r\n10. Obtain approval from another team member.\r\n11. Resolve all review comments.\r\n12. Ensure all required checks pass.\r\n13. Merge the Pull Request into `main` using a merge commit.\r\n14. Close the issue.\r\n15. Delete the completed branch.\r\n16. Move the Project board item to `Done`.\r\n17. Create a version tag when the relevant milestone is complete.\r\n\r\n## 15. Methodology Review and Change Control\r\n\r\nThis methodology is intended to remain in use for the duration of the project.\r\n\r\nThe team will not change the methodology merely because another process appears more convenient or because individual team members prefer a different workflow. Consistent use is necessary to maintain an understandable repository history and provide reliable evidence of the teamâ€™s development process.\r\n\r\nThe methodology may only be changed where there is clear evidence that the current process is causing significant or repeated problems. Examples include:\r\n\r\n- repeated merge conflicts caused by the workflow;\r\n- substantial delays in reviewing or integrating work;\r\n- a Gitea limitation that prevents the methodology from being followed;\r\n- a process requirement that creates unnecessary work without providing value;\r\n- difficulty tracing issues to their implementation; or\r\n- a project change that makes the existing methodology unsuitable.\r\n\r\nBefore changing the methodology:\r\n\r\n1. The problem must be discussed by the full team.\r\n2. Evidence of the problem must be identified.\r\n3. The proposed change and its expected benefit must be explained.\r\n4. The change must be approved by a majority of the team.\r\n5. The decision must be recorded in the project documentation.\r\n6. Purpose\r\n\r\nThis document defines the Git methodology that will be followed throughout the development of the Sport Analytics Tool.\r\n\r\nThe methodology establishes:\r\n\r\n- when commits must be created;\r\n- how commit messages must be written;\r\n- when branches must be created;\r\n- how branches must be named;\r\n- when branches may be merged;\r\n- the requirements that must be met before merging;\r\n- when project versions must be created; and\r\n- how project versions must be named.\r\n\r\nThe purpose of the methodology is to maintain an organised repository, support effective collaboration, reduce merge conflicts, enable code review and provide traceability between requirements and their implementation.\r\n\r\nAll team members are required to apply this methodology consistently across all project repositories.\r\n\r\n## 2. Selected Methodology\r\n\r\nThe team will use **GitHub Flow adapted for Gitea**.\r\n\r\nUnder this methodology:\r\n\r\n1. `main` contains the latest reviewed and working version of the project.\r\n2. Each significant unit of work begins as a Gitea issue.\r\n3. A short-lived branch is created for the issue.\r\n4. Development is completed through small, meaningful commits.\r\n5. The branch, commits and Pull Request reference the issue.\r\n6. A Pull Request is reviewed before it is merged.\r\n7. Approved work is merged into `main`.\r\n8. Important milestone states are identified using Git tags.\r\n\r\nThis methodology was selected because it provides sufficient control, traceability and peer review without introducing unnecessary permanent branches or administrative processes.\r\n\r\nA more complex methodology, such as Git Flow, would require additional `develop`, `release` and `hotfix` branches. These branches are not necessary for the size, duration or release structure of this project.\r\n\r\nThe selected methodology is therefore intended to remain lightweight enough to be followed consistently by all team members.\r\n\r\n## 3. The `main` Branch\r\n\r\nThe `main` branch represents the latest integrated, reviewed and working version of the project.\r\n\r\nThe following rules apply to `main`:\r\n\r\n- Direct development on `main` is prohibited.\r\n- Direct pushes to `main` are prohibited.\r\n- Changes may only enter `main` through an approved Gitea Pull Request.\r\n- `main` must remain in a buildable and working state.\r\n- Force pushes to `main` are prohibited.\r\n- Required automated checks must pass before a Pull Request may be merged.\r\n- Milestone version tags may only be created from `main`.\r\n\r\nThe `main` branch will be protected using Giteaâ€™s branch-protection settings where these settings are available.\r\n\r\n## 4. Gitea Issues and Traceability\r\n\r\nEvery significant development task must begin as a Gitea issue.\r\n\r\nAn issue must contain:\r\n\r\n- a clear title;\r\n- a description of the required work;\r\n- acceptance criteria;\r\n- an assigned team member;\r\n- the relevant sprint milestone; and\r\n- appropriate labels.\r\n\r\nExamples of work that requires an issue include:\r\n\r\n- implementing a feature;\r\n- fixing a bug;\r\n- creating or changing an API endpoint;\r\n- changing the database schema;\r\n- adding automated tests;\r\n- configuring infrastructure or CI/CD;\r\n- completing substantial documentation; and\r\n- performing a technical investigation that will influence development.\r\n\r\nVery small corrections, such as correcting a spelling error, may be included in an existing relevant issue.\r\n\r\nEach significant change will follow the traceability chain below:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nGitea issue â†’ branch â†’ commits â†’ Pull Request â†’ merge\r\n```\r\n\r\nFor example, work related to issue `#12` would be recorded as follows:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nIssue:        #12 Validate event submissions\r\nBranch:       feat/12-validate-event-submissions\r\nCommit body:  Refs #12\r\nPull Request: #12 Validate event submissions\r\nPR body:      Closes #12\r\n```\r\n\r\nThis process allows the team to trace completed work back to its original requirement, implementation, review and final integration.\r\n\r\n## 5. When to Create a Branch\r\n\r\nA branch must be created when a team member begins work on a Gitea issue involving code, tests, configuration or substantial documentation.\r\n\r\nBefore creating a branch:\r\n\r\n1. The related Gitea issue must exist.\r\n2. The issue must have a clear description.\r\n3. The issue must contain acceptance criteria.\r\n4. The issue must have an assignee.\r\n5. The issue must be assigned to the relevant sprint milestone.\r\n6. The developer must update their local copy of `main`.\r\n\r\nThe branch must be created from the latest version of `main`.\r\n\r\n```bash\r\ngit switch main\r\ngit pull origin main\r\ngit switch -c feat/12-validate-event-submissions\r\n```\r\n\r\nA branch should normally address one Gitea issue.\r\n\r\nWhere two issues cannot reasonably be separated, both issue numbers must be identified in the Pull Request description.\r\n\r\nBranches must be short-lived. A normal branch should be completed within five working days. A branch may not remain open beyond the sprint in which it was created unless the delay and reason are recorded in the related issue.\r\n\r\nIf a branch becomes too large to review effectively, the work must be divided into smaller issues and branches.\r\n\r\n## 6. How to Name Branches\r\n\r\nBranch names must follow this format:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n<type>/<issue-number>-<short-description>\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe approved branch types are:\r\n\r\n| Type       | Purpose                                          |\r\n| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------ |\r\n| `feat`     | New functionality                                |\r\n| `fix`      | Correction of incorrect behaviour                |\r\n| `docs`     | Documentation changes                            |\r\n| `test`     | Test creation or modification                    |\r\n| `refactor` | Code restructuring without a change in behaviour |\r\n| `chore`    | Maintenance, setup or configuration              |\r\n| `ci`       | Continuous integration or deployment changes     |\r\n\r\nExamples include:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nfeat/12-validate-event-submissions\r\nfix/18-prevent-duplicate-statistics\r\ndocs/21-add-api-documentation\r\ntest/24-test-event-validation\r\nrefactor/31-extract-statistics-service\r\nchore/7-configure-project\r\nci/9-add-backend-pipeline\r\n```\r\n\r\nBranch names must:\r\n\r\n- use lowercase letters;\r\n- contain the related issue number;\r\n- separate words using hyphens;\r\n- contain no spaces;\r\n- use a concise but meaningful description; and\r\n- reflect the main purpose of the branch.\r\n\r\n## 7. When to Commit\r\n\r\nA commit must be created whenever one small, logically complete unit of work has been completed.\r\n\r\nEach commit must:\r\n\r\n- represent one identifiable change;\r\n- relate to the issue assigned to the branch;\r\n- leave the affected section of the project in a working state;\r\n- not knowingly introduce compilation or build failures;\r\n- not knowingly cause existing tests to fail;\r\n- exclude unrelated changes; and\r\n- be understandable independently of later commits.\r\n\r\nExamples of suitable commits include:\r\n\r\n- creating the fixture database model;\r\n- adding event-schema validation;\r\n- implementing one API endpoint;\r\n- correcting one calculation error;\r\n- adding tests for one endpoint;\r\n- updating the setup instructions for one service.\r\n\r\nA commit must not combine unrelated work. For example, a single commit should not contain an unrelated API feature, user-interface redesign and documentation rewrite.\r\n\r\nDevelopers must commit regularly and must not wait until an entire sprint or large feature has been completed before creating a commit.\r\n\r\nTemporary commits may be used while work is in progress. However, commits with unclear messages such as `WIP`, `fix stuff` or `more changes` must not remain in a branch submitted for final review.\r\n\r\n## 8. How to Write Commit Messages\r\n\r\nThe team will use a simplified Conventional Commit format.\r\n\r\nThe required format is:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n<type>(<scope>): <description>\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe scope may be omitted when it does not provide useful additional information:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n<type>: <description>\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 8.1 Approved Commit Types\r\n\r\n| Type       | Purpose                                           |\r\n| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------- |\r\n| `feat`     | Adds new functionality                            |\r\n| `fix`      | Corrects incorrect behaviour                      |\r\n| `docs`     | Changes documentation only                        |\r\n| `test`     | Adds or modifies tests                            |\r\n| `refactor` | Restructures code without changing behaviour      |\r\n| `chore`    | Changes maintenance, setup or configuration files |\r\n| `ci`       | Changes the CI/CD process                         |\r\n\r\n### 8.2 Commit Message Requirements\r\n\r\nThe commit description must:\r\n\r\n- begin with a lowercase verb;\r\n- state what the commit accomplishes;\r\n- be concise but specific;\r\n- use the imperative form; and\r\n- avoid vague descriptions.\r\n\r\nAcceptable commit messages include:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nfeat(api): add event submission endpoint\r\nfix(stats): prevent duplicate events from affecting totals\r\ntest(api): add invalid event submission cases\r\ndocs(setup): document local database configuration\r\nci: run backend tests on pull requests\r\n```\r\n\r\nUnacceptable commit messages include:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nupdated files\r\nfixed things\r\nmore work\r\nchanges\r\nfinal version\r\nstuff\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 8.3 Linking Commits to Issues\r\n\r\nEvery normal development commit must reference the related Gitea issue in its commit body.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nfeat(api): validate submitted event structure\r\n\r\nRefs #12\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe issue will normally be closed by the Pull Request rather than by an individual commit. This ensures that the issue remains open until all associated work has been reviewed and merged.\r\n\r\nMerge commits, automated dependency commits and automatically generated revert commits are exempt from the normal issue-reference requirement where a manual reference would not be appropriate.\r\n\r\n### 8.4 AI-Assisted Code\r\n\r\nWhere AI-generated code is included in a commit, the commit body must include the required tool and model attribution.\r\n\r\n```text\r\nfeat(api): validate submitted event structure\r\n\r\nRefs #12\r\nAssisted-by: ChatGPT-Web[GPT-5.6 Thinking]\r\n```\r\n\r\nOnly tools and models genuinely used in producing the code contained in that commit may be listed.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 9. Project Board\r\n\r\nThe Gitea Project board will use the following columns:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBacklog\r\nReady\r\nIn Progress\r\nIn Review\r\nBlocked\r\nDone\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 4.1 Backlog\r\n\r\nThe `Backlog` contains identified work that has not yet been selected for active development.\r\n\r\nAn item may remain in the backlog where:\r\n\r\n- it is not yet a current priority;\r\n- further stakeholder clarification is required;\r\n- the task is optional;\r\n- the task belongs to a future sprint; or\r\n- the task requires further investigation before it can be prepared.\r\n\r\n### 4.2 Ready\r\n\r\nThe `Ready` column contains work that is sufficiently defined and can be started.\r\n\r\nAn issue may only move to `Ready` when it meets the teamâ€™s Definition of Ready.\r\n\r\n### 4.3 In Progress\r\n\r\nThe `In Progress` column contains work currently being completed.\r\n\r\nEach team member should normally have no more than one main issue in progress at a time. Sprint Structure\r\n\r\nThe project will be organised around the following formal milestones:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nSprint 1\r\nSprint 2\r\nSprint 3\r\nFinal Submission\r\n```\r\n\r\nEach milestone period will be treated as a sprint.\r\n\r\nEvery sprint will include:\r\n\r\n1. sprint planning;\r\n2. continuous work tracking;\r\n3. weekly stakeholder interaction;\r\n4. a weekly team standup;\r\n5. development and review; and\r\n6. a brief sprint close-out.\r\n\r\nEach sprint will have a clear sprint goal that states the main outcome the team intends to achieve.\r\n\r\n## 6.
