The submitter interface coverage was documented with the assistance of\nCodex[GPT-5.6 Sol].\n\r\n\n===== docs/architecture/overview.md =====\r\n# Architecture overview\n\n## Context\n\nThe project requires a separate frontend and backend, a team-designed hand-written HTTP API, a database, a public documentation website, authentication through an established provider or library, CI/CD, automated testing, and a relevant external API integration.\n\n## Selected foundation\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n    User[Browser user] -->|HTTPS| Frontend[React frontend]\n    Consumer[External API consumer] -->|HTTPS + API credentials| API[Node.js HTTP API]\n    Frontend -->|JSON over HTTPS| API\n    API -->|SQL through server-side driver| DB[(PostgreSQL / Supabase-hosted Postgres)]\n    API -->|Server-side request| External[Relevant external API]\n    API --> Worker[Future background jobs]\n    Worker --> DB\n    Docs[Public MkDocs site] -. documents .-> Frontend\n    Docs -. documents .-> API\n    Docs -. documents .-> DB\n```\n\nA background worker is shown as a future deployment boundary for batch imports, large exports, and expensive derivations. It should only be introduced when asynchronous work is implemented; it is not required for the initial scaffold.\n\n## Components and responsibilities\n\n### React frontend\n\n- Render accessible and responsive user journeys.\n- Collect and perform user-friendly client-side validation.\n- Call only documented backend endpoints for application data.\n- Handle loading, empty, error, unauthorised, and offline/unreachable states.\n- Never contain database credentials or authoritative business rules.\n\n### Node.js backend\n\n- Expose the versioned hand-written HTTP API.\n- Validate input and authenticate/authorise protected requests.\n- Enforce submitter scope, review workflows, traceability, and business rules.\n- Read and write the database through server-side repositories.\n- Call the external API while controlling credentials, retries, timeouts, and failure handling.\n- Produce stable error responses, logs, metrics, and audit evidence.\n\n### Shared contracts package\n\n- Hold request/response and event schemas shared across applications.\n- Provide TypeScript types derived from validation schemas.\n- Contain no database access, secrets, business logic, or authorisation decisions.\n\n### Database\n\n- Store source event data, submissions, review/correction history, definitions, derived results, and releases.\n- Enforce integrity with constraints and transactions.\n- Support traceability and efficient filtered queries through deliberate indexes.\n\n### Documentation site\n\n- Publish architecture, API, database, setup, testing, dependencies, security, deployment, methodology, and AI-use documentation.\n- Remain publicly accessible without requiring an account.\n\n## Data flow\n\n1. An approved submitter uploads or sends event data to the backend API.\n2. The backend authenticates the submitter and checks their authorised competition scope.\n3. The backend validates the payload against the versioned event schema.\n4. Valid data is staged or stored transactionally; invalid data returns actionable errors.\n5. Accepted event changes trigger only the dependent statistic calculations.\n6. Published API responses and dataset releases retain provenance to submissions, events, and definition versions.\n7. The frontend and external consumers obtain data from the backend API, never directly from generated database endpoints.\n\n## Security boundaries\n\n- Treat all browser and external-consumer input as untrusted.\n- Keep provider secrets, database credentials, external API keys, and service tokens server-side.\n- Use an established authentication provider/library; do not create password hashing, reset tokens, or session cryptography from scratch.\n- Authorise every protected route based on backend-verified identity and role/scope.\n- Rate-limit public/consumer endpoints before exposing them broadly.\n- Do not log credentials, tokens, full sensitive payloads, or unnecessary personal data.\n\n## Deployment boundaries\n\nThe frontend, backend, database, and documentation site must be independently deployable. The initial Azure deployment design is documented under `infra/azure/` and must be updated once exact services are selected and tested.\n\n## Trade-offs\n\nA monorepo simplifies shared tooling, atomic Pull Requests, and contracts while preserving separate deployable applications. Its main risk is accidental coupling. The folder boundaries, backend-only database rule, and CI checks must be enforced during review.\n\r\n\n===== docs/architecture/system-architecture.md =====\r\n# System architecture and development roadmap\n\n**Status:** Target architecture; foundation components are implemented, while later-tier\ncomponents are explicitly marked as planned.  \n**Related issues:** #38, #73\n**Last updated:** 12 August 2026\n\n## 1. Purpose and architectural principles\n\nThe Sport Analytics Tool is an event-driven cricket analytics platform. It accepts\ntraceable match-event submissions, validates and stores accepted events, derives statistics\nfrom those events, and publishes results through a web application, dataset exports, and a\nversioned HTTP API.\n\nThe design follows these principles:\n\n1. The React frontend and Express backend are separate applications and separate deployment\n   units. They communicate through the documented HTTP API.\n2. The handwritten backend is the only application-data boundary. The frontend and external\n   consumers never use database-generated REST or GraphQL endpoints.\n3. PostgreSQL event records are the source of truth. Published statistics are derived values,\n   not independently entered totals.\n4. Authentication proves identity; backend authorisation separately determines roles,\n   approval state, and competition, season, or fixture scope.\n5. Every submission, correction, statistic, and export must retain provenance.\n6. Basic functionality is delivered before asynchronous, cached, live, or user-defined\n   functionality is introduced.\n7. Planned components must not be presented as implemented. The architecture can grow by\n   adding workers and adapters without replacing the frontend, API, or event model.\n\n## 2. Current decisions and terminology\n\nThe approved event model covers T20 cricket. The current data source is Cricsheet, and the\nagreed scope recorded in ADR-003 is eleven franchise competitions plus men's and women's T20\ninternationals. The exact required statistic catalogue is still a dependency of issue #37.\n\n### Authentication provider\n\nThe project uses **Supabase Auth** as its managed authentication foundation, with\n**Google OAuth** as the initial sign-in provider.\n\nADR-004 supersedes the earlier Firebase decision in ADR-002. The repository now implements\nSupabase token verification in the Express backend using\n`supabase.auth.getUser(accessToken)`. Firebase Authentication is therefore not part of the\ncurrent runtime architecture and must not be implemented alongside Supabase Auth.\n\nThe authentication flow is:\n\n1. The React frontend initiates the managed Google OAuth flow through Supabase Auth.\n2. Supabase Auth issues a user session and access token.\n3. The frontend sends the access token to the handwritten Express API using a bearer token.\n4. The backend verifies the token with Supabase Auth.\n5. The backend maps the verified provider subject to the application's own account, role,\n   approval state and scoped permissions.\n\nAuthentication and authorisation remain separate:\n\n- **Supabase Auth** proves the user's identity.\n- **The Sport Analytics backend** determines what the user is allowed to do.\n\nApplication users are identified using the provider-neutral combination:\n\n```text\n(auth_provider, auth_subject)\n```\n\nThis prevents authentication-provider details from becoming coupled to competition, event,\nsubmission or statistic data.\n\nThe written lecturer ruling currently stored in the repository explicitly approves using\nSupabase as hosted PostgreSQL while avoiding its generated data API. It does not explicitly\nmention Supabase Auth.\n\nSupabase Auth is therefore the team's selected and implemented authentication foundation.\nAny required stakeholder or lecturer confirmation for its production use must remain\nrecorded as an open compliance decision until confirmed.\n\n## 3. High-level architecture\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart TB\n    subgraph Clients[Clients]\n        User[Browser user]\n        Consumer[External API or dataset consumer]\n    end\n\n    subgraph Applications[Separate deployable applications]\n        Frontend[React and Vite frontend]\n        API[Handwritten Express API<br/>/api/v1]\n    end\n\n    Auth[Supabase Auth<br/>current managed identity provider]\n    External[External data or sports API<br/>adapter and source provenance]\n\n    subgraph Data[Persistent data]\n        DB[(PostgreSQL<br/>events, users, grants, statistics, audit)]\n        Files[(Object storage<br/>planned for uploads and exports)]\n    end\n\n    subgraph Future[Intermediate and advanced components]\n        Queue[[Job queue or transactional outbox]]\n        Worker[Batch and derivation worker]\n        Cache[(Cache)]\n        Live[Live event provider]\n        Definitions[Versioned custom statistic definitions]\n    end\n\n    User -->|HTTPS| Frontend\n    Frontend -->|Managed sign-in| Auth\n    Frontend -->|HTTPS: JSON, multipart, bearer token| API\n    Consumer -->|HTTPS: public or API credentials| API\n    Consumer <-->|Versioned dataset files| Files\n    API -->|Verify access token| Auth\n    API -->|TLS SQL through server-side driver| DB\n    API -->|Upload and signed download operations| Files\n    API -->|Timeouts, quotas, retries| External\n    API -.->|Enqueue durable work| Queue\n    Queue -.-> Worker\n    Worker -.-> DB\n    Worker -.-> Files\n    API -.-> Cache\n    Worker -.->|Invalidate or refresh| Cache\n    Live -.->|Webhook, stream, or polling adapter| API\n    Definitions -.-> Worker\n```\n\nSolid connections are Basic-tier boundaries or selected foundations. Dotted connections are\nIntermediate or Advanced additions. Object storage is shown as planned because PostgreSQL\nshould store file metadata and provenance, not necessarily large source and export objects.\nIts provider has not yet been selected.\n\n### Trust boundaries\n\n- Browser input, uploaded files, external API responses, and consumer requests are untrusted.\n- The backend API is the policy-enforcement point for validation, authorisation, business\n  rules, quotas, and audit logging.\n- Authentication-provider configuration safe for a browser may be exposed through frontend\n  environment variables; database credentials, elevated auth keys, external API secrets, and\n  storage credentials remain server-side.\n- Only the backend and future workers connect to PostgreSQL or object storage with write\n  privileges.\n- Workers use the same domain services and validation rules as synchronous API operations;\n  asynchronous execution must not create a second set of business rules.\n\n## 4. Authorisation model\n\nThe minimum target model combines role-based access control with scoped grants. Role names\nremain subject to group approval, but the capabilities and separation of duties below should\nbe preserved.\n\n| Actor              | Typical permissions                                                                                                                                |\n| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Public viewer      | Read published fixtures, statistics, and public dataset-release metadata.                                                                          |\n| Registered user    | Public-viewer access plus account functions and their own submission history where applicable.                                                     |\n| Approved submitter | Create submissions only within explicit competition, season, and optionally fixture grants; view their own validation results; submit corrections. |\n| Reviewer           | Inspect validation evidence and accept or reject submissions within assigned scope; cannot silently rewrite source events.                         |\n| Administrator      | Approve or suspend submitters, manage roles and scoped grants, and audit decisions. Administrative actions are themselves audited.                 |\n| API consumer       | Read only the endpoints and datasets allowed by its API credential and quota; it receives no user or submission privilege by default.              |\n\nAn approved submitter is not just a role. The backend must require all of the following:\n\n```text\nverified identity\nAND active application account\nAND approved-submitter capability\nAND active scoped grant covering the target competition/season/fixture\nAND route-specific permission\n```\n\nThe implemented persistence foundation extends `app_user` with submitter approval state and\nlast-authenticated time, plus `submitter_competition_scope` grants. Approval-management work may\nlater add approver, reason, revocation, and expiry audit fields without changing the route-policy\nboundary. Denied checks return `403 Forbidden`; missing, invalid, expired, or revoked identity\ntokens return `401 Unauthorized`. The frontend may hide unavailable actions for usability, but\nfrontend state is never an authorisation control.\n\n## 6. Authentication and authorisation flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor User\n    participant UI as React frontend\n    participant Auth as Supabase Auth\n    participant API as Express API\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\n\n    User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\n    UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\n    Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\n    UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\n    API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\n    alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\n        API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\n    else Verified provider identity\n        Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\n        API->>DB: Upsert app_user; load status, role, approval, and scoped grants\n        alt Account or permission check fails\n            API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\n        else Route and resource scope allowed\n            API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\n            API-->>UI: Safe response\n        end\n    end\n```\n\nImportant controls are:\n\n- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\n- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\n- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\n- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\n- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\n  if supported by the selected provider;\n- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\n  narrow administrative operations that require them; and\n- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\n\n## 7. Event submission to calculated statistics\n\n### End-to-end flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor Submitter\n    participant UI as Frontend or API client\n    participant API as Handwritten API\n    participant AuthZ as Auth and permission middleware\n    participant Validate as Validation service\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\n    participant Jobs as Worker or in-process derivation\n    participant Files as File and export storage\n\n    Submitter->>UI: Enter events or choose JSON file\n    UI->>API: Submit payload, schema version, and bearer token\n    API->>AuthZ: Verify identity, approval, and target scope\n    AuthZ-->>API: Allowed submitter and effective scope\n    API->>API: Enforce content type and size, then calculate checksum\n    API->>DB: Create RECEIVED submission with provenance\n    opt Raw source file retained\n        API->>Files: Store source object under generated identifier\n    end\n    API->>Validate: Structural, referential, sequence, and cricket-rule validation\n    alt Validation fails\n        Validate-->>DB: Store safe field and record-level errors\n        API-->>UI: 422 with actionable validation result\n    else Valid but review required\n        Validate-->>DB: Mark PENDING_REVIEW\n        API-->>UI: 202 with submission status\n    else Accepted by policy or reviewer\n        Validate->>DB: Transactionally insert immutable event revisions and audit decision\n        DB-->>Jobs: Recalculate affected statistic scopes\n        Jobs->>DB: Read accepted current events\n        Jobs->>Jobs: Apply versioned deterministic definitions\n        Jobs->>DB: Upsert derived results and provenance\n        Jobs-->>API: Calculation complete or durable job status\n        API-->>UI: Accepted submission and statistic links\n    end\n```\n\nFor the Basic tier, bounded submissions and required fixture statistics may be validated and\nderived synchronously. Before processing becomes asynchronous, event acceptance and job\ncreation must be made atomic with a transactional outbox or equivalent pattern so an accepted\nevent cannot exist without its recalculation job.\n\n### Validation layers\n\n1. **Transport:** HTTPS, supported media type, request/file size, filename handling, and\n   decompression limits.\n2. **Contract:** versioned JSON schema, required fields, types, ranges, and unknown-field\n   policy.\n3. **Reference:** stable competition, fixture, team, and player identifiers; no name-based\n   player joins.\n4. **Cricket semantics:** innings/delivery ordering, team membership, extras, wickets,\n   super-over flags, miscounted overs, outcome forms, and other approved vocabulary.\n5. **Idempotency:** source reference, revision, checksum, and natural event identity prevent\n   duplicate ingestion while allowing corrections.\n6. **Permission:** submitter grant covers every target resource in the submission.\n7. **Review:** policy determines whether a structurally valid submission can be auto-accepted\n   or needs an independent reviewer.\n\nValidation errors are stored against the submission and returned without exposing internal\nqueries or secrets. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\naccepted records or none of them.\n\n### Corrections and derivation\n\nDelivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\nlive revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\nreads only the approved current-event view.\n\nRequired statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. The engine must cover\nthe event-model rules already approved in #27, including wides and balls faced, bowler extras,\nnon-boundary flags, innings-level penalty runs, actual legal-ball counts, stable player IDs,\nbowler-credit dismissal kinds, and the agreed super-over convention.\n\nEach stored result identifies:\n\n- statistic definition and version;\n- scope, such as fixture, innings, player, season, or career;\n- input event revision set or reproducible data version;\n- calculation status and timestamp; and\n- value and units.\n\nA correction marks only dependent results stale, recalculates them, and invalidates matching\ncache keys. Consumers must never observe a cache entry for a superseded data/definition\nversion.\n\n## 8. Files, datasets, and external integration\n\n### Uploads and source artefacts\n\n- Uploads enter through the backend; the browser never receives storage write credentials.\n- The API allow-lists formats, sanitises display names, ignores client filesystem paths,\n  generates object identifiers, enforces compressed and expanded size limits, and calculates\n  SHA-256 checksums.\n- PostgreSQL stores the submission, checksum, media type, object reference, source/retrieval\n  metadata, validation status, and owner. Object storage holds large bytes when selected.\n- Duplicate checksums are not sufficient by themselves: source reference and source revision\n  determine whether a file is a replay, correction, or different fixture.\n- Retention, malware scanning, and deletion rules must be agreed before arbitrary public file\n  uploads are enabled.\n\n### Dataset exports\n\nSmall filtered exports may stream from the API. Large or full releases become worker jobs and\nreturn `202 Accepted` with a status URL. Completed immutable releases include a version,\nscope, creation time, schema/statistic-definition versions, row or event counts, licence and\nprovenance notes, and checksums. Downloads use short-lived authorised links where necessary;\npublic releases may use stable public links.\n\n### External integration\n\nCricsheet's JSON archive is the approved historical source and already has a reproducible\ndownload and manifest process. It is a file feed, not a substitute for the project's required\nruntime external API integration. The team must select a relevant API based on stakeholder\nvalue, licence, T20 coverage, quotas, correction behaviour, and testability.\n\nAll providers are isolated behind adapters that convert external payloads into the internal\nsubmission contract. Provider calls use secret management, explicit timeouts, bounded retries\nwith jitter, rate-limit handling, circuit breaking where appropriate, schema checks, and\nobservable failures. Raw provider references, retrieval time, licence, version, and checksum\nare retained for provenance. An unavailable provider must degrade only the dependent feature,\nnot health checks, historical statistics, or unrelated API routes.\n\n## 9. Layout and spacing\n\n### 11.1 Spacing scale\n\nUse a 4 px base unit:\n\n```text\n4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 80\n```\n\n### 11.2 Recommended content widths\n\n| Context                           | Maximum width |\n| --------------------------------- | ------------: |\n| Analytics application             |       1600 px |\n| Documentation / long-form content |       1100 px |\n| Form-focused flow                 |        760 px |\n| Standard modal                    |    720â€“900 px |\n\n### 11.3 Grid\n\nDesktop analytical screens may use a 12-column grid.\n\nUseful patterns include:\n\n- 8 columns for primary match content and 4 for supporting events;\n- 9 columns for charts and 3 for compact supporting tables;\n- four equal KPI cards;\n- full-width tables when comparison is the primary task.\n\n### 11.4 Responsive behaviour\n\nUse content-driven breakpoints. Shape and surface language\n\n### 12.1 Corners\n\n| Element                   | Radius |\n| ------------------------- | -----: |\n| Inputs and small controls |   6 px |\n| Standard cards            |  10 px |\n| Large overlays            |  16 px |\n\nFully rounded pills are reserved for controls or statuses where the shape has a clear purpose.\n\n### 12.2 Signature clipped corner\n\nFeatured match cards, logo tiles and selected hero surfaces may use one clipped bottom-right corner.\n\nDo not apply clipped corners to every container.\n\n### 12.3 Borders and elevation\n\n- Use 1 px borders for structural separation.\n- Use shadows to communicate elevation, not decoration.\n- Day Match shadows are broad and low-opacity.\n- Night Match shadows are restrained and dark.\n- Avoid glowing card borders.\n- Avoid glassmorphism as the standard card language.\n\n### 12.4 Crease line\n\nA 2â€“3 px line is a recurring visual device.\n\nAppropriate uses:\n\n- active navigation;\n- selected KPI card;\n- chart target or benchmark;\n- score transition;\n- section accent.\n\nDo not use it between every row.\n\n---\n\n## 13. indefinite full-page spinner where useful structure can be rendered immediately.\n\n---\n\n## 14. Cricket data visualisation\n\n### 14.1 Chart palette\n\n| Role                    | Day Match       | Night Match     |\n| ----------------------- | --------------- | --------------- |\n| Current/selected series | Crease Green    | Powerplay Lime  |\n| Comparison series       | Analysis Cyan   | Review Cyan     |\n| Historical/unselected   | Scorebook Grey  | Commentary Grey |\n| Wicket/anomaly          | Boundary Orange | Boundary Orange |\n| Invalid/error state     | Rejected Red    | Rejected Red    |\n\n### 14.2 Chart rules\n\n- Start with the analytical question, not the chart type.\n- Avoid rainbow palettes.\n- Use line style, marker shape or opacity in addition to colour.\n- State units and ranges explicitly.\n- Label decisive points directly where practical.\n- Keep tooltips keyboard accessible where practical.\n- Provide text equivalents for important conclusions.\n- Do not delay access to data while a decorative animation completes.\n\n### 14.3 Cricket-specific conventions\n\nApproved visual patterns include:\n\n- orange wickets or decisive events;\n- green/lime for the selected innings or player;\n- cyan for comparison data;\n- a crease line for a target or benchmark;\n- ordered delivery events entering in source order.\n\nDo not use an error colour simply because it matches a team kit.\n\n---\n\n## 15. Motion system\n\n### 15.1 Motion character\n\n**Sharp acceleration, controlled stop.**\n\nMotion should make the interface feel responsive rather than decorative.\n\n### 15.2 Timing\n\n| Interaction            |   Duration |\n| ---------------------- | ---------: |\n| Hover / press feedback |  90â€“140 ms |\n| Tooltip / dropdown     | 140â€“180 ms |\n| Card / row entry       | 180â€“240 ms |\n| Page transition        | 220â€“320 ms |\n| Chart reveal           | 300â€“500 ms |\n| Modal opening          | 220â€“280 ms |\n\n### 15.3 Easing\n\n```css\n--ease-fast: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1);\n--ease-hit: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);\n```\n\n### 15.4 Signature animations\n\n#### Score update\n\n1. Old value moves up by no more than 4 px and fades.\n2. New value enters from below.\n3. The crease line flashes once.\n4. Total duration stays below 500 ms.\n\n#### Delivery insertion\n\nA new delivery enters with:\n\n- 6â€“8 px vertical movement;\n- short opacity transition;\n- no layout-blocking delay.\n\n#### Wicket\n\nUse one orange pulse or narrow strike.\n\nDo not shake the screen or use confetti.\n\n#### Page transition\n\nFade and move the primary content by no more than 8 px.\n\nDo not move persistent navigation.\n\n#### Chart reveal\n\nThe selected line may draw left-to-right once on first appearance.\n\nFiltering or refreshing data should update promptly rather than replay a long entrance sequence.\n\n### 15.5 Motion restrictions\n\nDo not:\n\n- bounce cards continuously;\n- use decorative parallax behind data;\n- stagger a dashboard for long periods;\n- animate every value on every render;\n- block interaction while an animation finishes;\n- change layout dimensions significantly on hover.\n\n### 15.6 Reduced motion\n\nRespect the userâ€™s reduced-motion preference:\n\n```css\n@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {\n  *,\n  *::before,\n  *::after {\n    animation-duration: 0.001ms !important;\n    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;\n    transition-duration: 0.001ms !important;\n    scroll-behavior: auto !important;\n  }\n}\n```\n\n---\n\n## 16. Accessibility\n\nAccessibility is a project requirement and must be designed in from the start.\n\nThe teamâ€™s UI target is **WCAG 2.2 AA** unless a stricter project requirement supersedes it.\n\n### 16.1 Required practices\n\n- Verify text/background colour contrast.\n- Provide a visible keyboard focus state.\n- Prefer semantic HTML before adding ARIA.\n- Keep interactive controls keyboard operable.\n- Do not communicate state by colour alone.\n- Provide text alternatives for meaningful images.\n- Respect reduced-motion preferences.\n- Maintain usable touch targets.\n- Support browser zoom without loss of function.\n- Preserve table and chart meaning on small screens.\n- Test light and dark themes independently.\n\n### 16.2 Colour notes\n\nThe muted light-theme text token has been darkened to `#627078` so it remains suitable for normal-size text against the Warm Canvas.\n\nBoundary Orange is a brand accent on light surfaces, not a normal small-text colour.\n\nStatus colours should normally be paired with readable neutral text rather than used as the only text colour.\n\n### 16.3 Focus treatment\n\nUse a clearly visible 2 px focus ring with a 2 px offset.\n\nPreferred rings:\n\n- Day Match: Crease Green or Analysis Cyan.\n- Night Match: Powerplay Lime or Review Cyan.\n\n---\n\n## 17. Iconography and imagery\n\n### 17.1 Icons\n\nUse:\n\n- simple outline icons;\n- consistent stroke weight;\n- consistent view-box sizing;\n- labels or accessible names for critical actions.\n\nAvoid mixing unrelated filled, outline and illustration styles.\n\n### 17.2 Cricket imagery\n\nPrefer:\n\n- real data;\n- scorecards;\n- field diagrams;\n- delivery trajectories;\n- the approved player mark;\n- licensed authentic photography where useful.\n\nAvoid:\n\n- generic trophy graphics;\n- crossed bats;\n- decorative shields;\n- fake 3D cricket balls;\n- arbitrary stadium imagery;\n- AI-generated players presented as real athletes.\n\n### 17.3 Photography\n\nWhen photography is used:\n\n- preserve authentic colours;\n- give overlaid text a solid or sufficiently opaque surface;\n- avoid heavy colour grading that competes with data;\n- do not place the logo over a face or visually complex focal point.\n\n---\n\n## 18. Implementation rules\n\n- Components use semantic tokens rather than raw theme hex values.\n- Theme selection belongs at application/provider level rather than inside individual cards.\n- Shared component structure and behaviour remain identical across themes.\n- New colours require a documented design reason.\n- New animation patterns require review for consistency and reduced-motion behaviour.\n- Use existing shared UI patterns before adding visually equivalent alternatives.\n- User-facing changes must be checked for responsiveness and accessibility before being considered done.\n- Brand assets must not contain secrets, runtime configuration or environment-specific URLs.\n- The frontend must not use branding work as a reason to bypass the documented HTTP API boundary.\n\n---\n\n## 21. Sprint Close-Out\n\nAt the end of each sprint, the team will complete a brief sprint close-out.\n\nThe Tuesday stakeholder meeting closest to the sprint deadline will be used to:\n\n- demonstrate completed work;\n- confirm whether completed work meets stakeholder expectations;\n- collect final feedback for the sprint;\n- identify incomplete work;\n- identify known defects and limitations; and\n- confirm how incomplete or changed work will be handled.\n\nDuring the final Thursday standup of the sprint, the team will briefly reflect on:\n\n1. what worked well;\n2. what caused difficulty; and\n3. one improvement that should be applied during the next sprint.\n\nThe sprint close-out does not require a separate meeting.\n\nA short sprint close-out record will be saved in the repository.\n\n```markdown\n# Sprint Close-Out\n\n**Sprint:**  \n**Date:**  \n**Attendees:**\n\n## Sprint Goal\n\n## Completed Work\n\n## Incomplete Work\n\n## Stakeholder Feedback\n\n## Known Defects and Limitations\n\n## Decisions\n\n## Improvement for the Next Sprint\n```\n\nOnly issues that meet the Definition of Done may be reported as completed.\n\nIncomplete work must be:\n\n- returned to the backlog;\n- moved to the next sprint with a documented reason;\n- divided into smaller issues; or\n- removed from scope with justification.\n\nThe agreed improvement must be reviewed during the following sprint to determine whether it was applied and whether it was effective.\n\n## 17. The submitter interface coverage was documented with the assistance of\nCodex[GPT-5.6 Sol].\n\r\n\n===== docs/architecture/overview.md =====\r\n# Architecture overview\n\n## Context\n\nThe project requires a separate frontend and backend, a team-designed hand-written HTTP API, a database, a public documentation website, authentication through an established provider or library, CI/CD, automated testing, and a relevant external API integration.\n\n## Selected foundation\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n    User[Browser user] -->|HTTPS| Frontend[React frontend]\n    Consumer[External API consumer] -->|HTTPS + API credentials| API[Node.js HTTP API]\n    Frontend -->|JSON over HTTPS| API\n    API -->|SQL through server-side driver| DB[(PostgreSQL / Supabase-hosted Postgres)]\n    API -->|Server-side request| External[Relevant external API]\n    API --> Worker[Future background jobs]\n    Worker --> DB\n    Docs[Public MkDocs site] -. documents .-> Frontend\n    Docs -. documents .-> API\n    Docs -. documents .-> DB\n```\n\nA background worker is shown as a future deployment boundary for batch imports, large exports, and expensive derivations. It should only be introduced when asynchronous work is implemented; it is not required for the initial scaffold.\n\n## Components and responsibilities\n\n### React frontend\n\n- Render accessible and responsive user journeys.\n- Collect and perform user-friendly client-side validation.\n- Call only documented backend endpoints for application data.\n- Handle loading, empty, error, unauthorised, and offline/unreachable states.\n- Never contain database credentials or authoritative business rules.\n\n### Node.js backend\n\n- Expose the versioned hand-written HTTP API.\n- Validate input and authenticate/authorise protected requests.\n- Enforce submitter scope, review workflows, traceability, and business rules.\n- Read and write the database through server-side repositories.\n- Call the external API while controlling credentials, retries, timeouts, and failure handling.\n- Produce stable error responses, logs, metrics, and audit evidence.\n\n### Shared contracts package\n\n- Hold request/response and event schemas shared across applications.\n- Provide TypeScript types derived from validation schemas.\n- Contain no database access, secrets, business logic, or authorisation decisions.\n\n### Database\n\n- Store source event data, submissions, review/correction history, definitions, derived results, and releases.\n- Enforce integrity with constraints and transactions.\n- Support traceability and efficient filtered queries through deliberate indexes.\n\n### Documentation site\n\n- Publish architecture, API, database, setup, testing, dependencies, security, deployment, methodology, and AI-use documentation.\n- Remain publicly accessible without requiring an account.\n\n## Data flow\n\n1. An approved submitter uploads or sends event data to the backend API.\n2. The backend authenticates the submitter and checks their authorised competition scope.\n3. The backend validates the payload against the versioned event schema.\n4. Valid data is staged or stored transactionally; invalid data returns actionable errors.\n5. Accepted event changes trigger only the dependent statistic calculations.\n6. Published API responses and dataset releases retain provenance to submissions, events, and definition versions.\n7. The frontend and external consumers obtain data from the backend API, never directly from generated database endpoints.\n\n## Security boundaries\n\n- Treat all browser and external-consumer input as untrusted.\n- Keep provider secrets, database credentials, external API keys, and service tokens server-side.\n- Use an established authentication provider/library; do not create password hashing, reset tokens, or session cryptography from scratch.\n- Authorise every protected route based on backend-verified identity and role/scope.\n- Rate-limit public/consumer endpoints before exposing them broadly.\n- Do not log credentials, tokens, full sensitive payloads, or unnecessary personal data.\n\n## Deployment boundaries\n\nThe frontend, backend, database, and documentation site must be independently deployable. The initial Azure deployment design is documented under `infra/azure/` and must be updated once exact services are selected and tested.\n\n## Trade-offs\n\nA monorepo simplifies shared tooling, atomic Pull Requests, and contracts while preserving separate deployable applications. Its main risk is accidental coupling. Purpose and architectural principles\n\nThe Sport Analytics Tool is an event-driven cricket analytics platform. It accepts\ntraceable match-event submissions, validates and stores accepted events, derives statistics\nfrom those events, and publishes results through a web application, dataset exports, and a\nversioned HTTP API.\n\nThe design follows these principles:\n\n1. Denied checks return `403 Forbidden`; missing, invalid, expired, or revoked identity\ntokens return `401 Unauthorized`. The frontend may hide unavailable actions for usability, but\nfrontend state is never an authorisation control.\n\n## 6. Authentication and authorisation flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor User\n    participant UI as React frontend\n    participant Auth as Supabase Auth\n    participant API as Express API\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\n\n    User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\n    UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\n    Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\n    UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\n    API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\n    alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\n        API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\n    else Verified provider identity\n        Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\n        API->>DB: Upsert app_user; load status, role, approval, and scoped grants\n        alt Account or permission check fails\n            API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\n        else Route and resource scope allowed\n            API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\n            API-->>UI: Safe response\n        end\n    end\n```\n\nImportant controls are:\n\n- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\n- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\n- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\n- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\n- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\n  if supported by the selected provider;\n- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\n  narrow administrative operations that require them; and\n- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\n\n## 7. Event submission to calculated statistics\n\n### End-to-end flow\n\n```mermaid\nsequenceDiagram\n    actor Submitter\n    participant UI as Frontend or API client\n    participant API as Handwritten API\n    participant AuthZ as Auth and permission middleware\n    participant Validate as Validation service\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\n    participant Jobs as Worker or in-process derivation\n    participant Files as File and export storage\n\n    Submitter->>UI: Enter events or choose JSON file\n    UI->>API: Submit payload, schema version, and bearer token\n    API->>AuthZ: Verify identity, approval, and target scope\n    AuthZ-->>API: Allowed submitter and effective scope\n    API->>API: Enforce content type and size, then calculate checksum\n    API->>DB: Create RECEIVED submission with provenance\n    opt Raw source file retained\n        API->>Files: Store source object under generated identifier\n    end\n    API->>Validate: Structural, referential, sequence, and cricket-rule validation\n    alt Validation fails\n        Validate-->>DB: Store safe field and record-level errors\n        API-->>UI: 422 with actionable validation result\n    else Valid but review required\n        Validate-->>DB: Mark PENDING_REVIEW\n        API-->>UI: 202 with submission status\n    else Accepted by policy or reviewer\n        Validate->>DB: Transactionally insert immutable event revisions and audit decision\n        DB-->>Jobs: Recalculate affected statistic scopes\n        Jobs->>DB: Read accepted current events\n        Jobs->>Jobs: Apply versioned deterministic definitions\n        Jobs->>DB: Upsert derived results and provenance\n        Jobs-->>API: Calculation complete or durable job status\n        API-->>UI: Accepted submission and statistic links\n    end\n```\n\nFor the Basic tier, bounded submissions and required fixture statistics may be validated and\nderived synchronously. Before processing becomes asynchronous, event acceptance and job\ncreation must be made atomic with a transactional outbox or equivalent pattern so an accepted\nevent cannot exist without its recalculation job.\n\n### Validation layers\n\n1. **Transport:** HTTPS, supported media type, request/file size, filename handling, and\n   decompression limits.\n2. **Contract:** versioned JSON schema, required fields, types, ranges, and unknown-field\n   policy.\n3. **Reference:** stable competition, fixture, team, and player identifiers; no name-based\n   player joins.\n4. **Cricket semantics:** innings/delivery ordering, team membership, extras, wickets,\n   super-over flags, miscounted overs, outcome forms, and other approved vocabulary.\n5. **Idempotency:** source reference, revision, checksum, and natural event identity prevent\n   duplicate ingestion while allowing corrections.\n6. **Permission:** submitter grant covers every target resource in the submission.\n7. **Review:** policy determines whether a structurally valid submission can be auto-accepted\n   or needs an independent reviewer.\n\nValidation errors are stored against the submission and returned without exposing internal\nqueries or secrets. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\naccepted records or none of them.\n\n### Corrections and derivation\n\nDelivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\nlive revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\nreads only the approved current-event view.\n\nRequired statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. The engine must cover\nthe event-model rules already approved in #27, including wides and balls faced, bowler extras,\nnon-boundary flags, innings-level penalty runs, actual legal-ball counts, stable player IDs,\nbowler-credit dismissal kinds, and the agreed super-over convention.\n\nEach stored result identifies:\n\n- statistic definition and version;\n- scope, such as fixture, innings, player, season, or career;\n- input event revision set or reproducible data version;\n- calculation status and timestamp; and\n- value and units.\n\nA correction marks only dependent results stale, recalculates them, and invalidates matching\ncache keys. Consumers must never observe a cache entry for a superseded data/definition\nversion.\n\n## 8. Files, datasets, and external integration\n\n### Uploads and source artefacts\n\n- Uploads enter through the backend; the browser never receives storage write credentials.\n- The API allow-lists formats, sanitises display names, ignores client filesystem paths,\n  generates object identifiers, enforces compressed and expanded size limits, and calculates\n  SHA-256 checksums.\n- PostgreSQL stores the submission, checksum, media type, object reference, source/retrieval\n  metadata, validation status, and owner. Object storage holds large bytes when selected.\n- Duplicate checksums are not sufficient by themselves: source reference and source revision\n  determine whether a file is a replay, correction, or different fixture.\n- Retention, malware scanning, and deletion rules must be agreed before arbitrary public file\n  uploads are enabled.\n\n### Dataset exports\n\nSmall filtered exports may stream from the API. Large or full releases become worker jobs and\nreturn `202 Accepted` with a status URL. Completed immutable releases include a version,\nscope, creation time, schema/statistic-definition versions, row or event counts, licence and\nprovenance notes, and checksums. Downloads use short-lived authorised links where necessary;\npublic releases may use stable public links.\n\n### External integration\n\nCricsheet's JSON archive is the approved historical source and already has a reproducible\ndownload and manifest process. It is a file feed, not a substitute for the project's required\nruntime external API integration. The team must select a relevant API based on stakeholder\nvalue, licence, T20 coverage, quotas, correction behaviour, and testability.\n\nAll providers are isolated behind adapters that convert external payloads into the internal\nsubmission contract. Provider calls use secret management, explicit timeouts, bounded retries\nwith jitter, rate-limit handling, circuit breaking where appropriate, schema checks, and\nobservable failures. Raw provider references, retrieval time, licence, version, and checksum\nare retained for provenance. An unavailable provider must degrade only the dependent feature,\nnot health checks, historical statistics, or unrelated API routes.\n\n## 9. Developers use safe environment placeholders and either shared development\n  services or an approved isolated local stack.\n- **Development:** the frontend and backend currently target separate Azure App Services.\n  PostgreSQL is hosted by Supabase in Frankfurt and reached by the backend over the TLS\n  Supavisor session pooler. The documentation site is deployed separately to Cloudflare\n  Pages.\n- **Preview/test:** Pull Requests always receive CI verification. Automated per-PR application\n  previews are desirable but not yet established.\n- **Production:** service names, database plan/region, storage, secrets, observability,\n  backups, and rollback procedures require a production decision record before release.\n\nFrontend configuration contains only browser-safe API and auth settings. Backend settings\ncontain `DATABASE_URL`, auth verification settings, allowed origins, external API keys, and\nfuture queue/storage credentials. Gitea Action secrets or platform secret stores provide\ndeployment credentials. Before deployment is considered reliable, the pipeline must also:\n\n1. build MkDocs with `mkdocs build --strict`;\n2. correct the frontend/backend deployment path and workspace references so they match\n   `apps/frontend` and `apps/backend`;\n3. make deployments depend on the same green quality checks used for Pull Requests;\n4. run reviewed database migrations as an explicit, observable, and recoverable step rather\n   than on application startup;\n5. deploy immutable build output to the correct application;\n6. smoke-test frontend, API health, CORS, authentication callback, and database connectivity;\n7. record release identity and support rollback to the previous application version; and\n8. keep destructive migration changes backward-compatible across the deployment window.\n\nPath filters should deploy only affected units, while changes to contracts, root lockfiles,\nor shared configuration must trigger every dependent unit. Typography\r\n\r\n### 10.1 Font families\r\n\r\n| Role                                  | Font             |\r\n| ------------------------------------- | ---------------- |\r\n| Display headings and major statistics | Barlow Condensed |\r\n| Interface and body text               | IBM Plex Sans    |\r\n| API paths, IDs and technical values   | IBM Plex Mono    |\r\n\r\nApproved weights:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBarlow Condensed: 500, 600, 700\r\nIBM Plex Sans: 400, 500, 600\r\nIBM Plex Mono: 400, 500\r\n```\r\n\r\nProduction font loading must be treated as a documented frontend dependency. Prefer package-managed or self-hosted fonts over an undeclared third-party runtime dependency.\r\n\r\n### 10.2 Type scale\r\n\r\n| Style           | Size / line-height | Weight | Typical use            |\r\n| --------------- | ------------------ | -----: | ---------------------- |\r\n| Display         | 64 / 64            |    700 | Live score             |\r\n| Page heading    | 48 / 52            |    700 | Page title             |\r\n| Section heading | 30 / 34            |    600 | Dashboard section      |\r\n| Card heading    | 22 / 26            |    600 | Panel title            |\r\n| KPI value       | 40 / 42            |    600 | Key statistic          |\r\n| Body            | 16 / 24            |    400 | Main content           |\r\n| Small body      | 14 / 20            |    400 | Supporting content     |\r\n| Label           | 12 / 16            |    600 | Metadata               |\r\n| Technical       | 13 / 20            |    400 | Endpoint, ID, checksum |\r\n\r\n### 10.3 Typography rules\r\n\r\n- Use tabular numerals for scores, rates and data tables.\r\n- Use condensed typography for display values, not paragraphs.\r\n- Use uppercase only for short labels and compact navigation.\r\n- Keep normal body text at 16 px where practical.\r\n- Do not make every number lime or green.\r\n- Use IBM Plex Mono only where monospacing communicates meaning.\r\n- The logo wordmark is artwork; do not recreate it using Barlow Condensed.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 11. Layout and spacing\r\n\r\n### 11.1 Spacing scale\r\n\r\nUse a 4 px base unit:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 80\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 11.2 Recommended content widths\r\n\r\n| Context                           | Maximum width |\r\n| --------------------------------- | ------------: |\r\n| Analytics application             |       1600 px |\r\n| Documentation / long-form content |       1100 px |\r\n| Form-focused flow                 |        760 px |\r\n| Standard modal                    |    720â€“900 px |\r\n\r\n### 11.3 Grid\r\n\r\nDesktop analytical screens may use a 12-column grid.\r\n\r\nUseful patterns include:\r\n\r\n- 8 columns for primary match content and 4 for supporting events;\r\n- 9 columns for charts and 3 for compact supporting tables;\r\n- four equal KPI cards;\r\n- full-width tables when comparison is the primary task.\r\n\r\n### 11.4 Responsive behaviour\r\n\r\nUse content-driven breakpoints. Starting values:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nSmall:   below 640 px\r\nMedium:  640â€“899 px\r\nLarge:   900â€“1199 px\r\nWide:    1200 px and above\r\n```\r\n\r\nStack dashboard regions before shrinking typography below usable sizes.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 12. Shape and surface language\r\n\r\n### 12.1 Corners\r\n\r\n| Element                   | Radius |\r\n| ------------------------- | -----: |\r\n| Inputs and small controls |   6 px |\r\n| Standard cards            |  10 px |\r\n| Large overlays            |  16 px |\r\n\r\nFully rounded pills are reserved for controls or statuses where the shape has a clear purpose.\r\n\r\n### 12.2 Signature clipped corner\r\n\r\nFeatured match cards, logo tiles and selected hero surfaces may use one clipped bottom-right corner.\r\n\r\nDo not apply clipped corners to every container.\r\n\r\n### 12.3 Borders and elevation\r\n\r\n- Use 1 px borders for structural separation.\r\n- Use shadows to communicate elevation, not decoration.\r\n- Day Match shadows are broad and low-opacity.\r\n- Night Match shadows are restrained and dark.\r\n- Avoid glowing card borders.\r\n- Avoid glassmorphism as the standard card language.\r\n\r\n### 12.4 Crease line\r\n\r\nA 2â€“3 px line is a recurring visual device.\r\n\r\nAppropriate uses:\r\n\r\n- active navigation;\r\n- selected KPI card;\r\n- chart target or benchmark;\r\n- score transition;\r\n- section accent.\r\n\r\nDo not use it between every row.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 13. Core interface components\r\n\r\n### 13.1 Buttons\r\n\r\n#### Primary\r\n\r\nDay Match:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBackground: Crease Green\r\nText: white\r\n```\r\n\r\nNight Match:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nBackground: Powerplay Lime\r\nText: Night Match\r\n```\r\n\r\nUse one dominant primary action per local region.\r\n\r\n#### Secondary\r\n\r\nUse:\r\n\r\n- surface background;\r\n- visible border;\r\n- primary text;\r\n- primary-colour focus/hover treatment.\r\n\r\n#### Destructive\r\n\r\nUse error styling only for genuinely destructive actions.\r\n\r\nIrreversible actions require confirmation.\r\n\r\n### 13.2 Cards\r\n\r\nCards should:\r\n\r\n- use solid surfaces;\r\n- group related information;\r\n- have a clear hierarchy;\r\n- avoid unnecessary icons;\r\n- use spacing before heavy shadows.\r\n\r\nDo not create a card solely to place a border around one line of text.\r\n\r\n### 13.3 Navigation\r\n\r\n- Desktop may use a compact left rail or top navigation.\r\n- Mobile navigation must remain understandable without relying only on icon familiarity.\r\n- The active state uses a soft selected surface plus the crease-line accent.\r\n- Navigation remains stable during page transitions.\r\n\r\n### 13.4 Tables\r\n\r\n- Left-align entity names.\r\n- Right-align numeric values.\r\n- Use tabular numerals.\r\n- Use subtle row separators.\r\n- Keep long table headers sticky where helpful.\r\n- Support horizontal overflow deliberately on small screens.\r\n- Do not turn every value into a badge.\r\n\r\n### 13.5 Forms\r\n\r\n- Keep labels visible above inputs.\r\n- Placeholder text does not replace a label.\r\n- Validation identifies the exact issue and location.\r\n- Required/error state is not communicated by colour alone.\r\n- Submission flows must show progress and actionable validation results.\r\n\r\n### 13.6 Loading and system states\r\n\r\nEvery data-driven screen must have deliberate states for:\r\n\r\n- loading;\r\n- empty results;\r\n- validation failure;\r\n- general error;\r\n- unauthorised access;\r\n- unavailable/offline backend;\r\n- partial data where the API explicitly supports it.\r\n\r\nDo not use an indefinite full-page spinner where useful structure can be rendered immediately.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 14. Cricket data visualisation\r\n\r\n### 14.1 Chart palette\r\n\r\n| Role                    | Day Match       | Night Match     |\r\n| ----------------------- | --------------- | --------------- |\r\n| Current/selected series | Crease Green    | Powerplay Lime  |\r\n| Comparison series       | Analysis Cyan   | Review Cyan     |\r\n| Historical/unselected   | Scorebook Grey  | Commentary Grey |\r\n| Wicket/anomaly          | Boundary Orange | Boundary Orange |\r\n| Invalid/error state     | Rejected Red    | Rejected Red    |\r\n\r\n### 14.2 Chart rules\r\n\r\n- Start with the analytical question, not the chart type.\r\n- Avoid rainbow palettes.\r\n- Use line style, marker shape or opacity in addition to colour.\r\n- State units and ranges explicitly.\r\n- Label decisive points directly where practical.\r\n- Keep tooltips keyboard accessible where practical.\r\n- Provide text equivalents for important conclusions.\r\n- Do not delay access to data while a decorative animation completes.\r\n\r\n### 14.3 Cricket-specific conventions\r\n\r\nApproved visual patterns include:\r\n\r\n- orange wickets or decisive events;\r\n- green/lime for the selected innings or player;\r\n- cyan for comparison data;\r\n- a crease line for a target or benchmark;\r\n- ordered delivery events entering in source order.\r\n\r\nDo not use an error colour simply because it matches a team kit.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 15. Motion system\r\n\r\n### 15.1 Motion character\r\n\r\n**Sharp acceleration, controlled stop.**\r\n\r\nMotion should make the interface feel responsive rather than decorative.\r\n\r\n### 15.2 Timing\r\n\r\n| Interaction            |   Duration |\r\n| ---------------------- | ---------: |\r\n| Hover / press feedback |  90â€“140 ms |\r\n| Tooltip / dropdown     | 140â€“180 ms |\r\n| Card / row entry       | 180â€“240 ms |\r\n| Page transition        | 220â€“320 ms |\r\n| Chart reveal           | 300â€“500 ms |\r\n| Modal opening          | 220â€“280 ms |\r\n\r\n### 15.3 Easing\r\n\r\n```css\r\n--ease-fast: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1);\r\n--ease-hit: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 15.4 Signature animations\r\n\r\n#### Score update\r\n\r\n1. Old value moves up by no more than 4 px and fades.\r\n2. New value enters from below.\r\n3. The crease line flashes once.\r\n4. Total duration stays below 500 ms.\r\n\r\n#### Delivery insertion\r\n\r\nA new delivery enters with:\r\n\r\n- 6â€“8 px vertical movement;\r\n- short opacity transition;\r\n- no layout-blocking delay.\r\n\r\n#### Wicket\r\n\r\nUse one orange pulse or narrow strike.\r\n\r\nDo not shake the screen or use confetti.\r\n\r\n#### Page transition\r\n\r\nFade and move the primary content by no more than 8 px.\r\n\r\nDo not move persistent navigation.\r\n\r\n#### Chart reveal\r\n\r\nThe selected line may draw left-to-right once on first appearance.\r\n\r\nFiltering or refreshing data should update promptly rather than replay a long entrance sequence.\r\n\r\n### 15.5 Motion restrictions\r\n\r\nDo not:\r\n\r\n- bounce cards continuously;\r\n- use decorative parallax behind data;\r\n- stagger a dashboard for long periods;\r\n- animate every value on every render;\r\n- block interaction while an animation finishes;\r\n- change layout dimensions significantly on hover.\r\n\r\n### 15.6 Reduced motion\r\n\r\nRespect the userâ€™s reduced-motion preference:\r\n\r\n```css\r\n@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {\r\n  *,\r\n  *::before,\r\n  *::after {\r\n    animation-duration: 0.001ms !important;\r\n    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;\r\n    transition-duration: 0.001ms !important;\r\n    scroll-behavior: auto !important;\r\n  }\r\n}\r\n```\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 16. Accessibility\r\n\r\nAccessibility is a project requirement and must be designed in from the start.\r\n\r\nThe teamâ€™s UI target is **WCAG 2.2 AA** unless a stricter project requirement supersedes it.\r\n\r\n### 16.1 Required practices\r\n\r\n- Verify text/background colour contrast.\r\n- Provide a visible keyboard focus state.\r\n- Prefer semantic HTML before adding ARIA.\r\n- Keep interactive controls keyboard operable.\r\n- Do not communicate state by colour alone.\r\n- Provide text alternatives for meaningful images.\r\n- Respect reduced-motion preferences.\r\n- Maintain usable touch targets.\r\n- Support browser zoom without loss of function.\r\n- Preserve table and chart meaning on small screens.\r\n- Test light and dark themes independently.\r\n\r\n### 16.2 Colour notes\r\n\r\nThe muted light-theme text token has been darkened to `#627078` so it remains suitable for normal-size text against the Warm Canvas.\r\n\r\nBoundary Orange is a brand accent on light surfaces, not a normal small-text colour.\r\n\r\nStatus colours should normally be paired with readable neutral text rather than used as the only text colour.\r\n\r\n### 16.3 Focus treatment\r\n\r\nUse a clearly visible 2 px focus ring with a 2 px offset.\r\n\r\nPreferred rings:\r\n\r\n- Day Match: Crease Green or Analysis Cyan.\r\n- Night Match: Powerplay Lime or Review Cyan.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 17. Iconography and imagery\r\n\r\n### 17.1 Icons\r\n\r\nUse:\r\n\r\n- simple outline icons;\r\n- consistent stroke weight;\r\n- consistent view-box sizing;\r\n- labels or accessible names for critical actions.\r\n\r\nAvoid mixing unrelated filled, outline and illustration styles.\r\n\r\n### 17.2 Cricket imagery\r\n\r\nPrefer:\r\n\r\n- real data;\r\n- scorecards;\r\n- field diagrams;\r\n- delivery trajectories;\r\n- the approved player mark;\r\n- licensed authentic photography where useful.\r\n\r\nAvoid:\r\n\r\n- generic trophy graphics;\r\n- crossed bats;\r\n- decorative shields;\r\n- fake 3D cricket balls;\r\n- arbitrary stadium imagery;\r\n- AI-generated players presented as real athletes.\r\n\r\n### 17.3 Photography\r\n\r\nWhen photography is used:\r\n\r\n- preserve authentic colours;\r\n- give overlaid text a solid or sufficiently opaque surface;\r\n- avoid heavy colour grading that competes with data;\r\n- do not place the logo over a face or visually complex focal point.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 18. Interface writing\r\n\r\nThe product voice is direct, informed and calm.\r\n\r\nGood:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nExplore matches\r\nView delivery data\r\nCompare innings\r\nExport dataset\r\nSubmission awaiting review\r\n12 events failed validation\r\n```\r\n\r\nAvoid:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nDive into the action\r\nUnleash next-level insights\r\nOops! Something went wrong\r\nYour data journey starts here\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 18.1 Error copy\r\n\r\nError messages should state:\r\n\r\n1. what failed;\r\n2. where it failed;\r\n3. what the user can do;\r\n4. whether data was accepted or published.\r\n\r\nExample:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nDelivery 43 is missing a striker identifier.\r\nNo events from this submission were published.\r\nAdd the identifier and submit the corrected file.\r\n```\r\n\r\n### 18.2 Cricket terminology\r\n\r\nUse recognised cricket terminology accurately.\r\n\r\nIf a term is likely to be unfamiliar to a general user, explain it with supporting copy or a tooltip rather than replacing it with vague language.\r\n\r\n---\r\n\r\n## 19. Purpose and architectural principles\r\n\r\nThe Sport Analytics Tool is an event-driven cricket analytics platform. It accepts\r\ntraceable match-event submissions, validates and stores accepted events, derives statistics\r\nfrom those events, and publishes results through a web application, dataset exports, and a\r\nversioned HTTP API.\r\n\r\nThe design follows these principles:\r\n\r\n1. The React frontend and Express backend are separate applications and separate deployment\r\n   units. They communicate through the documented HTTP API.\r\n2. The handwritten backend is the only application-data boundary. The frontend and external\r\n   consumers never use database-generated REST or GraphQL endpoints.\r\n3. PostgreSQL event records are the source of truth. Published statistics are derived values,\r\n   not independently entered totals.\r\n4. Authentication proves identity; backend authorisation separately determines roles,\r\n   approval state, and competition, season, or fixture scope.\r\n5. Every submission, correction, statistic, and export must retain provenance.\r\n6. Basic functionality is delivered before asynchronous, cached, live, or user-defined\r\n   functionality is introduced.\r\n7. Planned components must not be presented as implemented. The architecture can grow by\r\n   adding workers and adapters without replacing the frontend, API, or event model.\r\n\r\n## 2. Current decisions and terminology\r\n\r\nThe approved event model covers T20 cricket. The current data source is Cricsheet, and the\r\nagreed scope recorded in ADR-003 is eleven franchise competitions plus men's and women's T20\r\ninternationals. The exact required statistic catalogue is still a dependency of issue #37.\r\n\r\n### Authentication provider\r\n\r\nThe project uses **Supabase Auth** as its managed authentication foundation, with\r\n**Google OAuth** as the initial sign-in provider.\r\n\r\nADR-004 supersedes the earlier Firebase decision in ADR-002. The repository now implements\r\nSupabase token verification in the Express backend using\r\n`supabase.auth.getUser(accessToken)`. Firebase Authentication is therefore not part of the\r\ncurrent runtime architecture and must not be implemented alongside Supabase Auth.\r\n\r\nThe authentication flow is:\r\n\r\n1. The React frontend initiates the managed Google OAuth flow through Supabase Auth.\r\n2. Supabase Auth issues a user session and access token.\r\n3. The frontend sends the access token to the handwritten Express API using a bearer token.\r\n4. The backend verifies the token with Supabase Auth.\r\n5. The backend maps the verified provider subject to the application's own account, role,\r\n   approval state and scoped permissions.\r\n\r\nAuthentication and authorisation remain separate:\r\n\r\n- **Supabase Auth** proves the user's identity.\r\n- **The Sport Analytics backend** determines what the user is allowed to do.\r\n\r\nApplication users are identified using the provider-neutral combination:\r\n\r\n```text\r\n(auth_provider, provider_subject)\r\n```\r\n\r\nThis prevents authentication-provider details from becoming coupled to competition, event,\r\nsubmission or statistic data.\r\n\r\nThe written lecturer ruling currently stored in the repository explicitly approves using\r\nSupabase as hosted PostgreSQL while avoiding its generated data API. Authorisation model\r\n\r\nThe minimum target model combines role-based access control with scoped grants. Role names\r\nremain subject to group approval, but the capabilities and separation of duties below should\r\nbe preserved.\r\n\r\n| Actor              | Typical permissions                                                                                                                                |\r\n| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\r\n| Public viewer      | Read published fixtures, statistics, and public dataset-release metadata.                                                                          |\r\n| Registered user    | Public-viewer access plus account functions and their own submission history where applicable.                                                     |\r\n| Approved submitter | Create submissions only within explicit competition, season, and optionally fixture grants; view their own validation results; submit corrections. |\r\n| Reviewer           | Inspect validation evidence and accept or reject submissions within assigned scope; cannot silently rewrite source events.                         |\r\n| Administrator      | Approve or suspend submitters, manage roles and scoped grants, and audit decisions. Administrative actions are themselves audited.                 |\r\n| API consumer       | Read only the endpoints and datasets allowed by its API credential and quota; it receives no user or submission privilege by default.              |\r\n\r\nAn approved submitter is not just a role. The backend must require all of the following:\r\n\r\n```text\r\nverified identity\r\nAND active application account\r\nAND approved-submitter capability\r\nAND active scoped grant covering the target competition/season/fixture\r\nAND route-specific permission\r\n```\r\n\r\nThe target persistence model extends `app_user` with auditable grant records containing a\r\nscope, status, approver, reason, creation time, and optional expiry. Denied checks return\r\n`403 Forbidden`; missing, invalid, expired, or revoked identity tokens return\r\n`401 Unauthorized`. The frontend may hide unavailable actions for usability, but frontend\r\nstate is never an authorisation control.\r\n\r\n## 6. Authentication and authorisation flow\r\n\r\n```mermaid\r\nsequenceDiagram\r\n    actor User\r\n    participant UI as React frontend\r\n    participant Auth as Supabase Auth\r\n    participant API as Express API\r\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\r\n\r\n    User->>UI: Start managed Google sign-in\r\n    UI->>Auth: OAuth request with approved redirect URI\r\n    Auth-->>UI: Session and access token\r\n    UI->>API: Protected request with Bearer token\r\n    API->>Auth: Verify token using getUser(token)\r\n    alt Token missing, invalid, expired, or revoked\r\n        API-->>UI: 401 Unauthorized\r\n    else Verified provider identity\r\n        Auth-->>API: Stable provider subject\r\n        API->>DB: Load app_user, status, role, and scoped grants\r\n        alt Account or permission check fails\r\n            API-->>UI: 403 Forbidden\r\n        else Route and resource scope allowed\r\n            API->>DB: Execute transaction and append audit evidence\r\n            API-->>UI: Safe response\r\n        end\r\n    end\r\n```\r\n\r\nImportant controls are:\r\n\r\n- accept bearer tokens only over HTTPS and never log them;\r\n- validate identity on the backend rather than trusting decoded browser claims;\r\n- re-check permissions for every protected request and target resource;\r\n- prevent users from approving their own submitter status or expanding their own scope;\r\n- require step-up or recent authentication for destructive account or administration actions\r\n  if supported by the selected provider;\r\n- keep elevated provider credentials in the backend secret store and use them only for the\r\n  narrow administrative operations that require them; and\r\n- audit role, grant, review, correction, and account-status changes with actor and timestamp.\r\n\r\n## 7. Event submission to calculated statistics\r\n\r\n### End-to-end flow\r\n\r\n```mermaid\r\nsequenceDiagram\r\n    actor Submitter\r\n    participant UI as Frontend or API client\r\n    participant API as Handwritten API\r\n    participant AuthZ as Auth and permission middleware\r\n    participant Validate as Validation service\r\n    participant DB as PostgreSQL\r\n    participant Jobs as Worker or in-process derivation\r\n    participant Files as File and export storage\r\n\r\n    Submitter->>UI: Enter events or choose JSON file\r\n    UI->>API: Submit payload, schema version, and bearer token\r\n    API->>AuthZ: Verify identity, approval, and target scope\r\n    AuthZ-->>API: Allowed submitter and effective scope\r\n    API->>API: Enforce content type and size, then calculate checksum\r\n    API->>DB: Create RECEIVED submission with provenance\r\n    opt Raw source file retained\r\n        API->>Files: Store source object under generated identifier\r\n    end\r\n    API->>Validate: Structural, referential, sequence, and cricket-rule validation\r\n    alt Validation fails\r\n        Validate-->>DB: Store safe field and record-level errors\r\n        API-->>UI: 422 with actionable validation result\r\n    else Valid but review required\r\n        Validate-->>DB: Mark PENDING_REVIEW\r\n        API-->>UI: 202 with submission status\r\n    else Accepted by policy or reviewer\r\n        Validate->>DB: Transactionally insert immutable event revisions and audit decision\r\n        DB-->>Jobs: Recalculate affected statistic scopes\r\n        Jobs->>DB: Read accepted current events\r\n        Jobs->>Jobs: Apply versioned deterministic definitions\r\n        Jobs->>DB: Upsert derived results and provenance\r\n        Jobs-->>API: Calculation complete or durable job status\r\n        API-->>UI: Accepted submission and statistic links\r\n    end\r\n```\r\n\r\nFor the Basic tier, bounded submissions and required fixture statistics may be validated and\r\nderived synchronously. Before processing becomes asynchronous, event acceptance and job\r\ncreation must be made atomic with a transactional outbox or equivalent pattern so an accepted\r\nevent cannot exist without its recalculation job.\r\n\r\n### Validation layers\r\n\r\n1. **Transport:** HTTPS, supported media type, request/file size, filename handling, and\r\n   decompression limits.\r\n2. **Contract:** versioned JSON schema, required fields, types, ranges, and unknown-field\r\n   policy.\r\n3. **Reference:** stable competition, fixture, team, and player identifiers; no name-based\r\n   player joins.\r\n4. **Cricket semantics:** innings/delivery ordering, team membership, extras, wickets,\r\n   super-over flags, miscounted overs, outcome forms, and other approved vocabulary.\r\n5. **Idempotency:** source reference, revision, checksum, and natural event identity prevent\r\n   duplicate ingestion while allowing corrections.\r\n6. **Permission:** submitter grant covers every target resource in the submission.\r\n7. **Review:** policy determines whether a structurally valid submission can be auto-accepted\r\n   or needs an independent reviewer.\r\n\r\nValidation errors are stored against the submission and returned without exposing internal\r\nqueries or secrets. Multi-record acceptance is transactional: the database receives all\r\naccepted records or none of them.\r\n\r\n### Corrections and derivation\r\n\r\nDelivery event content is immutable. A correction inserts a new revision, marks the previous\r\nlive revision as superseded, and retains the original sequence and audit history. Derivation\r\nreads only the approved current-event view.\r\n\r\nRequired statistics begin with the group-approved catalogue from #37. The engine must cover\r\nthe event-model rules already approved in #27, including wides and balls faced, bowler extras,\r\nnon-boundary flags, innings-level penalty runs, actual legal-ball counts, stable player IDs,\r\nbowler-credit dismissal kinds, and the agreed super-over convention.\r\n\r\nEach stored result identifies:\r\n\r\n- statistic definition and version;\r\n- scope, such as fixture, innings, player, season, or career;\r\n- input event revision set or reproducible data version;\r\n- calculation status and timestamp; and\r\n- value and units.\r\n\r\nA correction marks only dependent results stale, recalculates them, and invalidates matching\r\ncache keys. Consumers must never observe a cache entry for a superseded data/definition\r\nversion.\r\n\r\n## 8. Files, datasets, and external integration\r\n\r\n### Uploads and source artefacts\r\n\r\n- Uploads enter through the backend; the browser never receives storage write credentials.\r\n- The API allow-lists formats, sanitises display names, ignores client filesystem paths,\r\n  generates object identifiers, enforces compressed and expanded size limits, and calculates\r\n  SHA-256 checksums.\r\n- PostgreSQL stores the submission, checksum, media type, object reference, source/retrieval\r\n  metadata, validation status, and owner. Object storage holds large bytes when selected.\r\n- Duplicate checksums are not sufficient by themselves: source reference and source revision\r\n  determine whether a file is a replay, correction, or different fixture.\r\n- Retention, malware scanning, and deletion rules must be agreed before arbitrary public file\r\n  uploads are enabled.\r\n\r\n### Dataset exports\r\n\r\nSmall filtered exports may stream from the API. Large or full releases become worker jobs and\r\nreturn `202 Accepted` with a status URL. Completed immutable releases include a version,\r\nscope, creation time, schema/statistic-definition versions, row or event counts, licence and\r\nprovenance notes, and checksums. Downloads use short-lived authorised links where necessary;\r\npublic releases may use stable public links.\r\n\r\n### External integration\r\n\r\nCricsheet's JSON archive is the approved historical source and already has a reproducible\r\ndownload and manifest process. It is a file feed, not a substitute for the project's required\r\nruntime external API integration. The team must select a relevant API based on stakeholder\r\nvalue, licence, T20 coverage, quotas, correction behaviour, and testability.\r\n\r\nAll providers are isolated behind adapters that convert external payloads into the internal\r\nsubmission contract. Provider calls use secret management, explicit timeouts, bounded retries\r\nwith jitter, rate-limit handling, circuit breaking where appropriate, schema checks, and\r\nobservable failures. Raw provider references, retrieval time, licence, version, and checksum\r\nare retained for provenance. An unavailable provider must degrade only the dependent feature,\r\nnot health checks, historical statistics, or unrelated API routes.\r\n\r\n## 9. Deployment and CI/CD\r\n\r\n```mermaid\r\nflowchart LR\r\n    Dev[Short-lived branch] --> PR[Gitea Pull Request]\r\n    PR --> CI[CI: install, structure, format,<br/>lint, typecheck, test, build]\r\n    CI --> Review[Peer review and approval]\r\n    Review --> Main[Protected main branch]\r\n    Main --> FE[Frontend deployment<br/>Azure App Service]\r\n    Main --> BE[Backend deployment<br/>Azure App Service]\r\n    Main --> Docs[MkDocs build and<br/>Cloudflare Pages deployment]\r\n    Migration[Reviewed SQL migrations] --> DB[(Supabase-hosted PostgreSQL)]\r\n    BE --> DB\r\n    FE --> BE\r\n    Secrets[Environment-specific secret stores] -.-> FE\r\n    Secrets -.-> BE\r\n```\r\n\r\n### Environments and deployment units\r\n\r\n- **Local:** Vite frontend on port 5173 and Express API on port 3000 run as separate\r\n  processes. Developers use safe environment placeholders and either shared development\r\n  services or an approved isolated local stack.\r\n- **Development:** the frontend and backend currently target separate Azure App Services.\r\n  PostgreSQL is hosted by Supabase in Frankfurt and reached by the backend over the TLS\r\n  Supavisor session pooler. The documentation site is deployed separately to Cloudflare\r\n  Pages.\r\n- **Preview/test:** Pull Requests always receive CI verification. Automated per-PR application\r\n  previews are desirable but not yet established.\r\n- **Production:** service names, database plan/region, storage, secrets, observability,\r\n  backups, and rollback procedures require a production decision record before release.\r\n\r\nFrontend configuration contains only browser-safe API and auth settings. Backend settings\r\ncontain `DATABASE_URL`, auth verification settings, allowed origins, external API keys, and\r\nfuture queue/storage credentials. Gitea Action secrets or platform secret stores provide\r\ndeployment credentials. Real secrets are never committed.\r\n\r\n### Pipeline controls\r\n\r\nThe existing Pull Request workflow uses Node.js 20, runs `npm ci`, then `npm run check`. The\r\nrepository check verifies required files, formatting, lint, TypeScript, automated tests, and\r\nall workspace builds. Before deployment is considered reliable, the pipeline must also:\r\n\r\n1. build MkDocs with `mkdocs build --strict`;\r\n2. correct the frontend/backend deployment path and workspace references so they match\r\n   `apps/frontend` and `apps/backend`;\r\n3. make deployments depend on the same green quality checks used for Pull Requests;\r\n4. run reviewed database migrations as an explicit, observable, and recoverable step rather\r\n   than on application startup;\r\n5. deploy immutable build output to the correct application;\r\n6. smoke-test frontend, API health, CORS, authentication callback, and database connectivity;\r\n7. record release identity and support rollback to the previous application version; and\r\n8. keep destructive migration changes backward-compatible across the deployment window.\r\n\r\nPath filters should deploy only affected units, while changes to contracts, root lockfiles,\r\nor shared configuration must trigger every dependent unit.
